title: Tool Passport: Molds That Report Themselves
one_liner: An OEM-owned, tamper-evident magnetic cycle counter and registry that makes every mold or die report its own location and shot count, so an unauthorized overrun shows up on the owner's screen and, in time, verified tools can be financed and insured.
customer: Wedge: US OEMs and PE-owned manufacturers ($50M-$500M) that have just moved, or are moving, tools out of China to US, Mexican, Vietnamese or Indian molders and never want a second breakup. Second user: the receiving nearshore molder, who installs the tag to earn 'verified' status with skittish customers. Later payers: tooling lenders, insurers and procurement teams that require a Passport.
problem: Even after reshoring, the OEM's tools sit in someone else's building with no independent record of how many shots they have run, on which press or when. The molder's own counters and MES data are self-reported. Enforcement is all after-the-fact forensics, which is expensive and easy to dispute. Because tools cannot be verified, they are worth nothing as collateral, cannot be insured on custody, and force OEMs into blunt contracts with minimum order quantities and amortization games.
solution: Phase 1 product, 'Tool Heartbeat', is a magnet-mount IP67 tag with an accelerometer that counts mold-open and mold-close cycles from vibration signatures, geofences the tool, detects removal, stores and forwards data over LTE-M, and reports to a per-tool 'passport': QR plate, serial, photo and fingerprint baseline, custody chain, shot ledger versus POs. Silence is contractually a breach. A model 'Tool Passport Addendum' for MSAs, drafted with a China-facing law firm, gives the OEM tag access and audit rights. Phase 2 uses the ledger as the meter for pay-per-shot billing and escrow, so the molder is paid per verified shot and proves innocence. Phase 3 is the registry as a standard: a VIN-and-Carfax for tools that lenders accept for collateral and underwriters use for custody cover. Phase 4 is Passport-backed tooling finance and custody insurance, where the balance-sheet upside sits. Tools still in China get the Census-and-forensics service from the parent, not tags, until SIM roaming and consent barriers are solved.
why_now: Reshoring has created thousands of just-moved tools whose owners are motivated to prevent a repeat. LTE-M and NB-IoT modules with IMUs now cost roughly $25-45 in BOM for a 3-5 year tag. EUROMAP 77 / OPC UA 40077 machine interfaces make molder-side data available to cross-check the independent witness. The tariff-driven wave of moves in 2025-26 (per the parent research) means a stock of new supplier relationships where the tag can be built into the contract from day one.
revenue_model: Hardware $150 per tag (roughly 60% margin at scale), $10 per tool per month for the ledger and alerts, and $1,000 per site onboarding (QR plates, fingerprint baseline, custody paperwork). A 60-tool OEM pays about $22k in year one and $7k a year after. Reaching $1M ARR takes about 140 OEM-sites, so the early business is small. The upside is in the standard: verified-tool finance fees and custody insurance premiums, plus a 'Passport Verified' seal for molders. This is a longer-dated bet, and the near-term money rests on services and hardware.
non_obvious_insight: The parent asks how to prove theft afterward. The inversion is that a tool is the only expensive asset in manufacturing that reports nothing about itself. A cycle count is a signal the tool already produces every 30 seconds through its own vibration, and no one owns it as a customer-side record. Once an independent meter exists, the honest molder benefits as much as the OEM, because it settles quantity disputes, proves clean custody and lets the molder offer pay-per-shot pricing. That aligned incentive is what makes a standard plausible, where a policing tool would not spread.
first_30_days: Weeks 1-3: build 10 prototype tags from an off-the-shelf LTE-M module and IMU (Blues Notecard-class) in a magnetic housing, about $3k. Validate cycle-count accuracy (target within 1%) on 2-3 presses at a friendly Ohio molder who gets free tags and 'Passport-ready' status. Weeks 2-4: pre-sell 3 OEM pilots at $2,400 for 10 tags plus a year of service with a refundable deposit, using the Reshoring Initiative and Ohio plant-manager networks. Draft the Addendum with one law firm. Use the $2,500 Marketplace Overrun Audit as the top-of-funnel cross-sell. Kill signal: vibration counting cannot reach 98% accuracy across press types, or fewer than 2 of 10 OEMs will sign a pilot.
lineage: mutation of I0552 ('Supplier Divorce Protection: Tool Census and Overrun Forensics'), type: 10x-or-inverted
competition_context:
Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: Harris Sliwoski (China Law Blog), Alitheon (FeaturePrint), Red Points, Corsearch (Zeal 2.0, Investigations 360, Distribution Control). White space: Coverage caveat: the WebSearch quota (200 per session) was already used up when I started, so I could not run the planned 6-12 searches. I also could not check Crunchbase, YC, Product Hunt, TechCrunch or open-source repos. The findings below come from about 25 direct page fetches, so treat 'nobody does this' as unproven. The vendors most likely missed are the many small China-based QC and sourcing agents that sell 'mold audits' and 'mold relocation', plus PI and investigation firms (Kroll-type). Do a manual pass on those before committing.

What I found: I found no productized, US-facing service that bundles (a) a serialized tool census, (b) cavity-level physical fingerprints, and (c) marketplace test-buy attribution of overruns to a specific tool. The problem is documented and treated as an unproductized legal-advice problem: Harris Sliwoski tells clients to keep an inventory form and audit quarterly, and never mentions a third-party vendor for it. Marketplace monitoring and takedown (Red Points, Corsearch, Alibaba's free IP platform) is commoditized and crowded. Object fingerprinting exists (Alitheon) but is aimed at electronics, aerospace and gray-market diversion, not tool-mark attribution.

Genuinely unserved: (1) cavity-level 'which tool made this part' attribution that holds up as evidence; (2) a tooling census standard for mid-market OEMs, timed to the exit window; (3) an evidence pack designed for counsel that a brand-protection vendor's screenshot-and-takedown workflow does not produce.

Weak points: Extraction (tool 3) is freight, customs and re-qualification work that sourcing agents and forwarders already do at low margin. Monitoring (tool 2, first half) is a commodity. Attribution is legally useful only when the overrun carries the client's IP (trademark, design patent, trade dress) and the client can enforce it. If the part is generic or unbranded, a match proves little. Chinese-court enforceability is unproven here. | How this version avoids them: Red Points and Corsearch operate on marketplaces after products have shipped. We work at the tool and stop overruns being made unseen, and we can hand them evidence. Alitheon authenticates individual items and has no way to know a tool's shot count or location, so their tech becomes a possible fingerprint tier. Harris Sliwoski tells clients to put permanent asset IDs on tools and audit quarterly. We productize that checklist into a continuous witness, and they are the natural channel for the Addendum. QIMA does periodic audits, so it becomes the install and spot-check subcontractor. MoldTrax and mold shot counters serve the molder's maintenance shop with self-reported data, while ours is customer-owned, independent and tamper-evident (whether other OEM-side products exist is unverified). Sourcify and sourcing agents are a channel, because provable custody helps their nearshore programs.

title: Unbundling Edits for Pet Insurance Claims
one_liner: Give pet insurers the claim-edit engine human health has had for 30 years: canonical procedure codes, bundling rules, and price benchmarks for messy vet invoices.
customer: Pet insurance MGAs, carriers and TPAs adjudicating roughly 100k to 2M claims a year, the mid-size players without in-house claims data science. Later, corporate veterinary groups and pet-owner pre-treatment estimate checks.
problem: Veterinary invoices are free-text line items exported from practice-management systems, with no universal procedure code set and no NCCI-style edits. Adjusters hand-review them. Insurers cannot tell that the vet billed anesthesia monitoring, an IV catheter, fluids and the e-collar as separate lines on top of a surgery fee, or what a routine dental cleaning costs in a given ZIP code. Claim severity is inflating with vet consolidation, and insurers answer with blanket premium hikes instead of line-level accuracy.
solution: An API that ingests invoice PDFs or line items. An LLM plus a hand-built taxonomy of the top ~300 vet procedures (about 80% of spend) normalizes each line to a canonical code. A rules layer, built the way NCCI and medically-unlikely edits work, flags unbundling, duplicates and implausible units. A benchmark layer returns usual-and-customary ranges by ZIP and practice type. The adjuster sees pay, reduce or review, with reason codes.
why_now: There are roughly 7 million insured US pets, and the segment is growing at double-digit rates with loss-ratio and price-hike pressure. Corporate vet consolidation is raising invoice complexity. LLMs make invoice line-item normalization, the hard part that took human-health edit vendors years, cheap enough for a two-person team.
revenue_model: Per-claim fee of $0.25-$0.75, or 10-15% of validated savings. A 500k-claim MGA is worth $150-350k a year. Add a benchmark-data license for vet chains and an owner-facing estimate checker later.
non_obvious_insight: Every automation wave in healthcare billing started with standardized codes and claim edits, not with AI. Cotiviti and Optum are basically edit libraries with sales teams. Pet insurance is at the pre-CPT stage. Someone who has spent years living inside code sets, bundling logic and 'this is included in the global fee' arguments can build the missing layer in weeks. Insurers will not fund a fight with vets. They will fund a neutral, consistent, explainable edit that does not vary by adjuster.
first_30_days: Recruit one ex-coder (CPC) and a vet tech consultant. Build the 300-line taxonomy from public estimate sheets and a few hundred sample invoices. Approach 10 pet-insurance MGAs and TPAs with a free retrospective: run 5,000 of their anonymized past invoices and report the dollar share found in bundled, duplicate or out-of-range lines. Convert the best result into a paid pilot on per-claim pricing.
lineage: original (tournament survivor)
competition_context:
Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: VetControl (Illingen, Germany), Five Sigma (Clive AI claims adjuster), Sirma (custom ML for PetsBest, now under Synchrony), FairVet. White space: Nobody I found sells a US, insurer-facing, explainable edit library (canonical line-item codes, bundling and duplicate rules, unit plausibility, reason codes) with cross-carrier benchmarks, to mid-size MGAs and TPAs.

- VetControl is the only true direct analog, and it is German, GOT-based, a services-plus-software hybrid, and shows no US customers.
- Five Sigma and Sirma classify line items for coverage, not for pricing or bundling.
- FairVet and Vet Receipt hold consumer-sourced benchmark data with no insurer-grade normalization.
- Trupanion and Lassie built in-house and are not customers.
- Verisk has standardized the policy side only.

The unserved gap is an invoice-derived, ZIP-level, procedure-level price index built from insurer claims, which no owner-upload app can match in volume. It would be joined to explainable pay/reduce/review decisions for mid-size carriers with no data science team.

Structural risk to flag. Human-health edits work because of provider contracts and CMS rules. Pet insurers have no contracts with vets and no 'global fee' concept, and they pay owners by reimbursement. Line-level reductions therefore land on policyholders as balance bills, which invites complaints and regulatory attention. I found no US insurer RFP or public spend for this. The demand evidence is indirect: cost inflation, plus vendors like VetControl selling a similar product in Germany.

title: Payable Bias Audit for Black Mass Sellers
one_liner: A fixed-price audit that measures, in euros per year, the systematic sampling bias between a black mass seller's protocol and its buyer's. The fix is then locked in as a sealed sample-of-record and a two-line contract clause.
customer: Wedge: independent mechanical pre-processors and EV/ESS dismantlers in Germany, Poland and Benelux. They sell roughly 300-3,000 t/yr of black mass (about EUR 1-8M/yr) to one or two hydromet buyers on a binding buyer-gate assay. About 40-60 such sellers exist in the corridor. The buyer of the audit is the owner, CFO or commercial director who signs the offtake contract, not the QA chemist. Gigafactory scrap desks come later, since they have in-house metallurgists and slow procurement.
problem: The parent sells noise reduction, but random sampling noise mostly nets out for a seller shipping 40-100 lots a year. What does not net out is systematic bias between two protocols. A grab from the top of a big bag or drum, an unrecorded moisture basis, and segregation of coarse Cu/Al foil against fine cathode powder all push in one direction on every lot, so bias moves money one way. A 3% payable bias on EUR 5M of annual sales is EUR 150k a year, invisible lot by lot. The umpire clause cannot catch it. Bureau Veritas's own umpire page (fetched this session) describes umpire work as its own analysis of samples, that is, a re-assay of the retained sample. If the retained sample carries the bias, the umpire confirms it. Sellers therefore concede, or split the difference, on lots they were systematically shorted on.
solution: Step 0 costs nothing. Ask the seller for 30-plus historical lots with its own dispatch assay and the buyer's settlement assay. A significant one-signed mean gap qualifies the prospect. It might be lab bias or sampling bias, and the audit separates the two. Step 1 is the Paired-Protocol Bias Audit, sold at EUR 20-30k. Over 8-10 lots, take three samples per lot: the seller's method, the buyer's documented method, and a Theory-of-Sampling incremental sample from a falling stream or drum auger, split by rotary divider into sealed triplicates. Blind full-digestion assays go to one accredited lab, with a 20% cross-check at a second. The deliverable is the bias with a confidence interval, the euros per year it costs, a Gy heterogeneity and sampling-variance statement, and a written seller Sampling Protocol of Record. Step 2 is a per-lot Sample-of-Record service using a portable kit of about EUR 15-25k (rotary divider, riffle splitters, balance, drying oven, inert glove bag). It gives sealed triplicates at load-out and a two-line clause: 'sample of record taken per Protocol v1, sampling variance not to exceed x% relative at 95%, retained split binds on dispute'. If the buyer refuses the clause, the seller holds the data to shop the volume to another recycler. No containerised station is built until an anchor customer pays for one.
why_now: Several Western recyclers restructured or were bought out in 2025 (Li-Cycle into Glencore, per the parent research), so sellers are already renegotiating counterparty terms and a new clause is on the table anyway. Delegated Regulation (EU) 2025/606 has been in force since 24 July 2025, and recyclers report annually to member-state authorities from 2026. Composition data for intermediate fractions such as black mass therefore has to be documented, which turns a written sampling protocol into a compliance artefact. Ni/Co price swings make each percentage point of payable worth more.
revenue_model: Audit fee of EUR 20-30k, with about EUR 10-12k of lab pass-through. Per-lot Sample-of-Record fee of EUR 900-1,800, or EUR 8-15 per tonne. Optional protocol licence to a buyer who wants to adopt the seller's protocol as its own. Year-1 target: 6 audits and 4 conversions at about 40 lots each, roughly EUR 350-400k revenue on about EUR 40k of kit. It is deliberately a small service business first, and the dataset of bias by protocol is the asset it builds.
non_obvious_insight: The value is the sign and size of the bias, not the reduction in variance. The party it costs is the natural buyer, and it is already identifiable from settlement history before any sampling. That makes the sales motion outbound and quantified (euros lost per year) instead of a vague accuracy pitch. A 'no bias found' result is also sellable, as a clean bill for lenders and counterparties. Because the umpire re-assays the same retained sample, no incumbent product is structured to detect the effect.
first_30_days: Week 1: retain a named senior sampling practitioner and an accredited partner lab. Anchor Protocol v1 to representative-sampling standards such as DS 3077 and, by analogy, ISO 12743 for concentrates. Both are recalled from memory, so verify. Build a one-page leak calculator from public payables and the seller's own settlement pairs. Weeks 2-3: send it to 40 named sellers in the DE/PL corridor and run the historical-pair test for every taker. Weeks 3-4: sign three audits at cost (about EUR 12k of pass-through each) in return for permission to publish anonymised results. Buy or lease a used rotary divider and portable kit. Go/no-go: at least 2 of 3 show a bias worth more than the audit fee, otherwise pivot to offspring 2 or 3.

title: Handoff Assay of Record for EU Recyclers
one_liner: A co-signed black mass assay with a stated uncertainty at each handoff from a first recycler to a hydromet plant, so both sides' EU Battery Regulation mass balances close. The regulated first recycler pays, on a compliance budget, not the seller in a settlement fight.
customer: First recyclers, meaning mechanical pre-processors that shred cells and modules and ship black mass on to hydromet. About 25-40 sites across the EU are in scope. The economic buyer is the head of compliance/EHS or the CFO. Secondary payers are the hydromet recycler, which co-pays for the input documentation it needs, and extended-producer-responsibility organisations that audit recycling chains.
problem: Delegated Regulation (EU) 2025/606 sets the calculation and verification methodology for recycling efficiency and material recovery. It was verified this session as in force from 24 July 2025, with annual data submission to the member-state authority from 2026 and first material-recovery targets due 31 December 2027. Secondary sources say it requires a mass balance of input, intermediate and output fractions with composition data, that black mass is an intermediate fraction, and that the first recycler must coordinate data across downstream treatment. Those points are not verified against the act text, and how input composition must be determined is unknown. Black mass therefore sits exactly at the joint. The pre-processor reports what it sent on, using its dispatch assay, and the hydromet reports what it received, using its receipt assay. When the two assays of the same lot differ by 5-15%, the chain shows phantom Co/Ni/Li losses or gains. The first recycler is blamed either way and cannot show whether it clears a recovery target.
solution: A Handoff Certificate per lot. A sealed sample-of-record is co-signed by both sites and assayed once by an accredited lab under a Gy-based protocol, with declared moisture basis and a stated sampling-variance component. Both sites use that single number. On top sits a Chain Reconciler, a small web tool. It ingests certificates plus mass and yield data, propagates the sampling variance through the delegated act's formulas by Monte Carlo, and outputs the documentation-format annual report. Recovery rates carry confidence intervals, for example 'Co recovery 91.3% plus or minus 3.1%, provably above target' or 'cannot demonstrate compliance'. The stage-1 recycler pays a certificate fee of EUR 350-700 per lot plus a EUR 25-60k annual site subscription. Stage-2 co-signs and pays a smaller receipt-side fee. Verifiers and PROs buy audit packs. Sampling is done by contracted crews with portable kits, so there is no station capex.
why_now: The first annual reporting cycle under the 2025 methodology is live in 2026, and the first 2027 recovery targets are 15 months out. That is when recyclers discover their handoff numbers do not reconcile. The methodology was only fixed in mid-2025, so any tool built for it is new. Black mass has also become a controlled, largely within-OECD flow (a secondary source cites Basel Annex VIII export limits), which makes a small, identifiable set of handoffs.
revenue_model: Subscription plus usage. Per-site ACV of EUR 40-90k for stage-1 sites, with lot certificates included up to a tier. Stage-2 receipt-side fees. PRO and verifier audit packs of EUR 20-50k. Ceiling of roughly EUR 1.2-2.7M ARR from 30 EU stage-1 sites, and more from hydromet co-pay and PRO packs. Later, recycled-content documentation for cell makers and OEMs, which phases in from about 2028 and needs verification, becomes a second, larger payer.
non_obvious_insight: The customer is not buying accuracy but consistency and a defensible uncertainty. For a regulator's mass balance, it matters more that both ends of a handoff quote the same number with a stated variance than that the number is perfect. A recycler at 91% against a 90% target cannot claim compliance without an uncertainty statement, and with one it can. The compliance owner has a different budget from commercial procurement, does not haggle over EUR 500 a lot, and prefers to have a third party on record. It is the same sampling insight, sold as risk cover instead of dispute settlement.
first_30_days: Days 1-5: read the delegated act's annexes and documentation template to confirm how input and intermediate composition is sourced, and kill or reshape the idea if it just accepts supplier-declared values. Days 5-20: ask 8 first recyclers for 12 months of black mass dispatch assays and hydromet receipt assays (both are on settlement statements). Run a free one-page Chain Gap Check that translates the assay gap into percentage points of reported Co/Ni/Li recovery. Days 20-30: convert 2-3 to six-month certificate pilots, and open talks with one environmental verifier or consultancy that would carry the Reconciler into its verification engagements.

title: The Reference Panel: Neutral Ruler for E/M Levels
one_liner: A neutral, triple-blind coder-and-physician panel that measures how reliable any E/M level really is, and sells that measurement to scribe vendors, payers and providers who are now fighting over it.
customer: Three sides. First payer: health-system and large-group compliance and counsel with contested encounters (payer record requests, downcode appeals, OIG inquiries). Second: scribe and coding-AI vendors that need independent validation. Third: payers running automated downcoding, which face state laws and regulator scrutiny on human review. Auditors and RCM firms become licensees.
problem: E/M level is a judgment, not a fact. Published studies show weak agreement even among trained coders: one study had five experienced certified coders assign codes to six notes and only one code was unanimous, and another found 36% inter-rater reliability among eight research nurses across 4,137 visits. Yet three AI systems now assign levels (scribes, autonomous coders, payer downcoders) and contradict each other. Each treats its own output as truth, and extrapolated overpayment demands multiply one reviewer's noise across a whole claims universe. Nobody publishes the noise floor, so the dispute goes to whoever has more lawyers.
solution: An independent panel of certified coders plus a physician advisor labels encounters blind against the 2021 MDM and time rules, with adjudication and published agreement statistics (Krippendorff's alpha by specialty and level). An AI pre-read and single coder handle easy cases and only disagreements escalate to a three-person panel, so the average is about 1.6 reviews per encounter. Product ladder: (a) 'Panel-Certified Level' files for contested encounters, giving a level, a confidence and dissent notes, at $60-90 each; (b) annual validation of a vendor's or payer's AI against a held-out panel-labeled set with a published scorecard, $75-200k a year; (c) noise-floor benchmark subscription and consortium membership at $25-50k; (d) later, a licensed evaluator model trained on the adjudicated labels. Governance rules that make it credible: published methodology, physician advisory board, no vendor equity, no single side above 30% of revenue.
why_now: In 2025-26 three sets of AI systems are assigning and contesting E/M levels at scale. Payers' automated downcoding (Cigna's nationwide policy from October 2025) is reported, as are state downcoding laws in Arkansas and Virginia, with more pending. Scribe vendors are advertising 'audit-ready' and 'verified' accuracy. The 'coding arms race' is in the literature. Each side needs a ground truth it can cite, and the trailing 12 months are when disputes and vendor procurement turn to evidence.
revenue_model: Contested-encounter certification at $60-90 per encounter is the first revenue, with cost near $15-25 including adjudication, so about 70% gross margin. Vendor and payer validation at $75-200k a year. Benchmark and consortium memberships at $25-50k a year. Later licensing of the evaluator model. Revenue mix goal is roughly a third from each of providers, vendors and payers to keep neutrality.
non_obvious_insight: The product is the disagreement rate. Once you can say 'certified coders disagree on this specialty's level-4 encounters 30% of the time', a single-reviewer downcode or a single-reviewer audit finding falls inside the noise floor, and an extrapolated overpayment should shrink, which is worth real money to providers. It also turns every incumbent into a customer. VMG, MDaudit, Healthicity, Charta and the AI coders can each validate against or license the panel, so none of them needs to see it as an attack. Credibility is the moat and scales with every adjudicated encounter.
first_30_days: Recruit 6 CPC/CPMA coders and one physician advisor. Approach two health-system compliance teams that have open payer record requests or downcode disputes and offer to triple-blind review 100 contested encounters each at a pilot rate ($8-15k). Publish a 6-page methodology paper and the first anonymized agreement statistics. Offer two scribe or coding-AI vendors a 200-encounter validation on the understanding that results are only published with consent. Aim for one paid pilot and one vendor letter of intent.
lineage: mutation of I0389 ('Independent Auditor for AI-Scribed Billing'), type: 10x-or-inverted
competition_context: Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: VMG Health (Compliance Risk Analyzer + AI Governance and Targeted Coding Audits), MDaudit, Healthicity (Audit Manager, Compliance Manager, E/M Analyzer/Utilization Benchmarking tool), Ambience Healthcare (scribe vendor with coding). White space: Nobody I found sells a scribe-specific, independent, coder-signed audit product. The gaps are: (1) An explicit before/after go-live drift baseline per provider, benchmarked against specialty peers and other scribe adopters. VMG's Compliance Risk Analyzer and Healthicity's E/M benchmarking do peer outlier analysis but are not framed around scribe go-live cohorts. (2) A review protocol built around what fails audits under the 2021 E/M rules: MDM and time attestations, not HPI/exam bloat. None of the vendor pages I read describe this. (3) An audit memo designed to be handed to a payer, auditor or OIG, plus a payer-downcoding forecast. (4) Independence from the scribe vendor, since Ambience, Abridge and DeepScribe all self-attest coding quality. (5) Scribe-agnostic coverage across a mixed-vendor group. Several legal write-ups recommend exactly the 'post-implementation baseline audit comparing AI-generated coding patterns against prior practice' (https://www.subjecttoinquiry.com/2026/06/ai-assisted-billing-could-create-fca-pitfalls-how-healthcare-companies-can-get-ahead-of-risk/), and none of the articles I read named a vendor that sells it. Caveat: this is a wedge in framing and packaging, not a technology moat. The existing audit firms and platforms (VMG, MDaudit, Healthicity) can run this same claims analysis and coder review, and could rebrand it 'AI scribe audit' within a quarter or two. My search was also incomplete, and startups from 2026 may exist that I did not surface. | How this version avoids them: It does not compete as another audit platform or AI coder. VMG Health, MDaudit and Healthicity run single-reviewer workflows for one side, so they cannot be neutral, and they are natural licensees and second-opinion buyers. Ambience (95% 'AAPC-verified'), Abridge and DeepScribe self-attest, and the panel is the independent replacement for that claim. Fathom, Arintra and CodaMetrix have the same conflict. title: Flight simulator drills for county SNAP eligibility workers
one_liner: Short daily drills using synthetic cases built from the state's own error taxonomy, sold to county social-services directors who are about to pay for every eligibility mistake.
customer: County social services / DSS directors and supervisors in county-administered SNAP states (NY, NC, CA, OH, MN, CO, VA) and the state associations of counties. Buyers pay $12k-25k per county per year, or $150-300 per worker. States can buy statewide at $150k-500k.
problem: H.R.1 raises the state/county share of SNAP administrative costs from 50% to 75% starting October 2026. From October 2027, states with payment error rates of 6% or higher must pay part of benefit costs. In New York, St. Lawrence County faces an extra $776,000 in year one, Jefferson County over $1 million and Warren County $415,000. The state's error rate is 13% against a 6% line, a penalty of about $1B statewide, described as 'a missile heading right at New York State'. North Carolina's error rate is 6.69%, with state cost-share exposure of about $140M at 5% and $420M at 15%. The state's advice to counties is 'documenting, documenting, documenting'.
solution: A 15-minute daily micro-drill for eligibility workers: a synthetic household case (pay stubs, shelter costs, household composition changes, address changes) with a realistic case-file packet, where the worker computes eligibility and benefit. The drill feeds back the exact error that federal QC would cite. Cases are generated from the state's policy manual and the public USDA QC error categories (wage reporting, household size, address changes and shelter deductions are the common ones), with no real client data. Supervisors see per-worker error-type heatmaps and a coaching queue. Later: an optional second-look review desk staffed by former QC reviewers that samples a county's real closed cases.
why_now: The error-rate look-back, cost-shift start (October 2026) and penalty tiers (October 2027) create a hard two-year clock. Louisiana is paying cash bonuses to error spotters, Kansas hired an outside consultant, Virginia is buying technology for error checking, and NC is running monthly QC webinars and targeting high-error counties. States are visibly buying error-reduction help, and there is no standard product for it.
revenue_model: Per-worker annual subscription ($150-300) or flat per-county fee ($12k-25k); statewide contracts through the state SNAP office or county association; add-on per-case second-look review at $18-30/case.
non_obvious_insight: A county with a 0% error rate is still penalized if the state averages above 6%, so no county can solve this alone and the real buyer is the state or the association pooling county money. Meanwhile individual county directors are hurting now and have discretionary admin budgets and training budgets they can spend without an RFP. Synthetic cases avoid the PII and system-access barrier that blocks most govtech vendors in benefits programs, so a small team can start selling in weeks, not after a FedRAMP-style review. Evidence: county exposure and 13% New York error rate (https://www.northcountrypublicradio.org/news/story/53929/20260910/snap-cost-shift-pushes-north-country-counties-into-a-financial-bind); NC official on documentation, targeted training and CQI (https://citizenportal.ai/articles/9949745/north-carolina/executive/organizations/state-departments-and-agencies/mental-health/developmental-disabilities-and-substance-abuse-services/state-official-urges-counties-to-cut-snap-payment-error-rate-to-avoid-hr1-cost-shares); state remediation tactics such as bonuses, outside consultants and new training (https://www.yahoo.com/news/articles/states-scramble-cut-snap-error-214614305.html).
first_30_days: Build 40 synthetic cases across the top error elements from one state's manual, with a scoring engine. Approach the state county association's SNAP resource group and 5 county DSS directors with a free 30-day pilot with a pre/post test on 10 new hires. Publish a 'your error rate in dollars' calculator for county commissioners. Convert the two most engaged counties to paid annual plans priced below their discretionary-purchase limits.

title: Grid-Code Models for AI Data Centers

Texas SB 6 and NERC large-load work now push for ride-through and dynamic models, but no standard model library or test lab exists for GPU cluster, power-supply and UPS stacks.

Sell per-project model packages, ride-through study reports and compliance-ready certification letters. Charge a subscription to keep models current as hardware changes.
why_now: Multi-GW campuses, NERC's large-load task force and Texas and PJM interconnection rules in 2025-26 are turning load models from optional into a gating item.
revenue_model: $75-300k per project for the model and study, an annual model-maintenance subscription, and test or certification fees paid by UPS and power-shelf OEMs.
non_obvious_insight: Everyone frames data centers as demand. The grid now treats them as a dynamic device, like a giant inverter-based generator. Inverter-generator modeling became a consulting industry after events like the 2016 Blue Cut fire, and large-load modeling will follow. The model library is the moat.

title: Orphan Fleet Depot for Bankrupt-Maker Electric Buses
one_liner: Sustainment-as-a-service for school districts and transit agencies stuck with electric buses whose manufacturer went bankrupt, using the military's orphan-platform playbook (salvaged parts pool, configuration control, depot repair, availability guarantees).
customer: School districts, regional education service agencies and small transit agencies that own buses from failed OEMs (Lion Electric US buses, Proterra, and similar EV truck and bus makers), plus state grant administrators and cooperative-purchasing bodies that want the taxpayer-funded fleets running.
problem: When Lion Electric went through bankruptcy and its new owner voided prior U.S. warranties, districts were left with buses nobody would service. Some sourced parts themselves, some sidelined buses, and some went back to diesel. Proterra's transit business went through a similar handoff. Grant-funded buses that sit idle are a political and audit embarrassment. Dealers cannot fix proprietary battery, inverter and charge-port faults, and there is no parts channel.
solution: Run it like a military orphan-platform sustainment program. (1) Buy the bankruptcy estate's remaining parts, tooling and diagnostics at liquidation. (2) Build a per-VIN configuration database and a reverse-engineered diagnostic library. (3) Stand up a regional depot and a mobile repair van for line-replaceable units: contactors, DC-DC converters, charge ports, battery management modules and pack modules. (4) Buy sidelined orphan buses cheaply as cannibalization donors. (5) Sell a fixed annual sustainment contract per bus that guarantees a morning-route availability rate, backed by a shared spares pool across districts sized with readiness-based sparing math.
why_now: Lion's sale voided U.S. warranties (reported late 2025), so the 2025-26 school year is when the pain became real. The installed base of grant-funded EV buses is large and aging out of warranty, and subsidy rollbacks (the federal commercial clean vehicle credit ended for vehicles acquired after Sept 30, 2025) make further OEM failures likely. The parts estates of failed makers are cheapest to buy right now, before anyone else sees their value.
revenue_model: Annual sustainment contract of roughly $4-8k per bus with an availability guarantee, plus time-and-materials for depot repairs, spares-pool membership fees for districts that want priority access, and salvage and refurbished battery pack sales. Sold through cooperative purchasing vehicles so districts do not each run a bid.
non_obvious_insight: Orphaned does not mean unfixable. In most orphaned fleets, 5-10 recurring line-replaceable units cause most of the downtime. A small shared spares pool plus a configuration-controlled baseline can lift availability from a coin flip to about 90%. The right buyer is not one district's bus garage but a state agency or regional service center pooling many districts, because the sparing math only works at fleet-of-fleets scale. Military sustainers call this the DMSMS problem and solved it by owning the baseline instead of waiting for the OEM.
first_30_days: Build a list of about 20 districts that took Lion or similar deliveries in 2022-24 from press coverage and grant award lists. Offer one district a free 'orphan health check' on a stranded bus using generic diagnostic tools and an EV-experienced transit mechanic. Register as a bidder in the relevant bankruptcy and liquidation processes and ask for the parts inventory lists. Hire 1-2 retired transit or heavy-duty EV technicians. Sign three districts to a per-bus quarterly pilot and use their fault logs to identify the top recurring failure modes.

title: Load Recovery for Municipal Utilities and Co-ops
one_liner: Sell the verified dead-plant record to the municipal electric utilities and rural co-ops that lose money every month the anchor plant sits dark, priced as a package plus a bonus tied to the load they get back.
customer: Municipal electric systems, rural electric co-ops and their joint-action agencies or statewide associations (for example American Municipal Power and the state municipal electric associations) in OH, PA, MI and IN, where an anchor industrial plant has closed and the utility's own economic-development or general manager decides. Wedge: 8 utilities in the Mahoning Valley, Akron/Canton and western PA with an idle plant of at least 2 MW in their territory.
problem: When a plant with several MW of load closes, a small public utility keeps paying its fixed wholesale power, transmission and substation costs but spreads them over fewer kWh, so rates rise for homes and shops and the remaining industrial customers get nervous (an assumption to validate with 10 utility managers). These utilities have no economic-development staff, are ignored by the investor-owned-utility databases and grid-analytics vendors, and cannot tell a data-center or battery developer what is actually inside the fence of their dead plant. Meanwhile the plant's energized service, which the utility itself installed and meters, is the one asset that could replace the lost load.
solution: A 'Load Recovery Package' per idle plant: (1) electrician-verified one-line diagram, gear nameplates, spare capacity and slab/crane condition; (2) the utility's own historical interval load and substation loading, which only the utility holds, turned into a stranded-load scorecard showing what re-energizing 2, 4 or 8 MW would do to fixed-cost recovery and rates; (3) a pre-cleared economic-development rate rider and a written will-serve position, drafted with the utility's engineer, which is the hardest input in the parent's product and is free when the utility is the customer; (4) outreach to a curated buyer list (manufacturers, battery and cold-storage operators, small data-center and inference developers) with the record as the data room. Later, a member-services version sold through a joint-action agency to all members.
why_now: Buyers with real money now want existing energized industrial shells, so a dead plant in a small utility's territory has more than one class of possible buyer for the first time in decades. Large-load tariffs and interconnection queues at the big investor-owned utilities push developers to look for capacity elsewhere, and roughly 128-week transformer lead times make existing service worth years. Ohio's 125+ local data-center moratoriums are a problem for pure data-center strategies, so a buyer-agnostic pitch to friendly municipal utilities is safer.
revenue_model: $9,500 per Load Recovery Package paid from the utility's economic-development budget; $18,000 per year retainer covering up to five sites, buyer outreach and a rolling record refresh; a capped performance bonus of about 10% of the first-year demand-charge margin from re-energized load (cap around $60k), structured as an economic-development services fee from the utility and not a commission on a property sale (have Ohio counsel confirm the real-estate licence question before signing). Channel: a joint-action agency or state association licenses the tool to members at $40k-$80k per year. Bottom-up: about 100-150 qualifying utilities in four states at an average $12k in year one is $1.2M-$1.8M, with 70-plus percent gross margin after the electrician cost on the package.
non_obvious_insight: The utility, not the broker or the manufacturer, is the party that already holds the two hardest inputs, years of interval meter data on the dead plant and the ability to say in writing what it would take to re-energize it, and it is also the only party that loses money every month the plant stays dark. Sell to them and the will-serve letter that costs the parent weeks of chasing becomes something the customer hands you. Small public utilities are also unserved by every funded competitor, which all chase hyperscalers and the big investor-owned utilities.
first_30_days: Week 1: build a list of every municipal electric system and co-op in northeast Ohio and western PA (from state association member lists) and match each to idle plants using Ohio EPA and county parcel data; shortlist 20 with a dark plant of at least 2 MW. Weeks 2-3: call 20 general managers and superintendents; pitch a free 'stranded-load scorecard' on their dead plant using their meter data. Get three to share interval data and access. Week 4: deliver one scorecard plus a paid quote of $9,500 for the full package, and pitch a 20-minute slot at a state municipal electric association meeting. Success test: one utility signs the $9,500 package or a letter of intent, and one association agrees to a member pilot.

title: Mother-Tongue Lifeline for Dementia Flashpoints
one_liner: On-demand live video calls where a dementia-trained speaker of the patient's first language and dialect coaches the English-speaking aide and calms the patient at bath, bedtime and exit-seeking moments.
customer: Home care agencies and PACE programs in immigrant-dense metros (NYC, LA, Miami, Chicago, Bay Area, Houston) with dementia clients whose aides do not share their language. Second: Medicaid managed long-term care and D-SNP plans. Third: families on a flat monthly plan.
problem: Bilingual and multilingual patients lose their second language as dementia advances and drift back to the language, dialect and idioms of their childhood. Agencies send whoever is available. The English-speaking aide cannot say the one calming phrase during the bath, so the bath fails, the patient panics, the aide gets hurt or quits, and the family blames the agency. Telephone interpretation lines translate literally, but a dementia patient's fragments and proverbs need to be validated, not translated. It is a communication problem, not an interpretation problem.
solution: A dedicated line, staffed on demand by trained bilingual retirees, nurses and teachers, covering the long tail: Yiddish, Haitian Creole, Toisanese, Cantonese, Polish, Russian, Uzbek, Punjabi, Tagalog, Greek, Armenian. A tablet or phone is propped where the patient can see it. The specialist speaks to the patient in dialect while coaching the aide in English in the earpiece: 'she's asking for her sister, say she is coming, then hum this song.' Sessions are 3-10 minutes at known flashpoints. Specialists are trained by aides in validation and redirection, not interpretation.
why_now: The post-war Soviet, Chinese, Caribbean and Southeast Asian immigrant cohorts who arrived in the 1960s-80s are now reaching moderate-to-severe dementia. Low-latency video is universal and cheap. AI companions such as KindredMind (voice clone of the caregiver, 12 languages, launched worldwide in May 2026) prove the demand, but they work best for mild cases and comfortable tech users. For moderate-to-severe dementia and live crises, the warm human voice in the right village dialect is the missing complement, and the agencies will pay per minute for it.
revenue_model: $1.25-1.75 per minute billed to agencies and plans, with 60-70 percent gross margin after specialist pay of about $0.45 per minute. Families get $129 per month for 20 sessions. Later, enterprise contracts with MLTC and D-SNP plans that cover the cost as a quality tool.
non_obvious_insight: Patients revert not just to a language but to a specific dialect and era, for example Toisanese, not Mandarin, and the idioms of 1955. A literal interpreter is useless because what calms is tone, a lullaby, a proverb and a familiar name. The buyer is not the family but the agency, which is desperate because language mismatch is why its aides quit its hardest cases. Nobody pays interpreters for companionship, so this talent pool of bilingual retirees is unmined and cheap.
first_30_days: Pick two languages with dense local demand, for example Toisanese or Cantonese in NYC and Haitian Creole in Miami. Recruit 10 bilingual retirees through churches, senior centers and community media. Train them in a one-page validation script. Run it on WhatsApp video with no software. Call 15 small agencies serving those communities and offer 30 free minutes per case. Sign the first three at $1.50 per minute with a $300 monthly minimum.

title: Finish Crew: Stranded Solar Job Completion
one_liner: A completion contractor that takes half-built solar jobs abandoned by bankrupt installers all the way to permission-to-operate, and is paid by the lenders whose loans go bad while the system sits dark.
customer: Solar loan originators and servicers, and TPO sponsors, that now hold stranded projects. The seven finance partners named in the Freedom Forever order are the first buyers: GoodLeap, EnFin, Credit Human, EverBright, Participate, Project Solar and Sunrun. Credit unions and ABS trustees holding 2023-2025 solar loans are the second wave. Homeowners are the beneficiary but do not pay.
problem: When a big installer dies, thousands of systems are left installed but not energized, or half-built. Freedom Forever went Chapter 11 in April 2026 and converted to Chapter 7 on Aug 7, 2026, with about 1,600 layoffs. The borrower stops paying a $30-50k loan on a roof that produces nothing. Lender, homeowner and dead installer each say it is someone else's job. The court let lenders hire new contractors and push systems to PTO, but a lender has no bench of crews and no playbook for doing it.
solution: Run the work as a records-recovery business first and a crew business second. For each stranded job, build a forensic pack: the AHJ permit file, the utility interconnection record, the design set from the dead company's design and CRM tools, equipment serials from distributors and consignment records, and a site photo audit. Sort jobs into tiers: paperwork-only (contractor of record and engineer's stamp need re-issuing), inspection fix, missing hardware, and never started (unwind and refund path). Price each tier at a fixed fee plus a bonus at PTO, and subcontract the labor to licensed local electricians and laid-off installer crews. Give the lender a dashboard of its whole stranded book with cost to cure and expected PTO date.
why_now: Freedom Forever's Chapter 7 conversion (Aug 2026, creditor claims due Oct 16, 2026) and the court order letting financiers step in make this concrete now. Sunnova (June 2025), SunPower (Aug 2024) and 100+ other solar failures came before it. Post-25D volume is down in 2026, so more failures are likely. Lenders have step-in rights but no operating capacity.
revenue_model: Fixed completion fee of $1.5-4k per job by tier, plus a $500 success bonus at PTO, paid by the lender or servicer. Add a monthly stranded-book dashboard subscription. Later, sell a 12-month workmanship warranty on completed jobs, paid by the lender, and a retainer for standby capacity when the next installer fails.
non_obvious_insight: A stranded job is 80% a records and legal-standing problem, not a labor problem. Permits, interconnection applications, engineer stamps and design files sit in a dead contractor's name and portal logins, so nobody can legally finish even though laid-off crews are cheap and plentiful.
