title: Special-Ed Parent Tracker Feeding Host-School Programs
one_liner: A $20-a-month IEP chief of staff for Texas parents whose service-minute logs identify the families and districts where a clinician-led, voucher-funded host-school program is the real solution.
customer: Texas parents of children with IEPs, reached through special-ed parent groups and pediatric practices, some holding Texas Education Freedom Account (TEFA) funds of about $10K, up to about $30K for IEP students at accredited private schools. Partner: small accredited private schools with empty classrooms. Supply: speech-language pathologists, BCBAs and dyslexia therapists.
problem: The parent tracker has a low-ARPU, high-CAC consumer business at $20 per month. The host-school program has a high-value payer but no cheap way to find qualified families or to decide where to site a cohort. Parents with documented missed services and a stalled district are stuck, and the money that could fix it is locked behind accreditation and a two-year operating history that they do not have.
solution: Parents upload the IEP and get a legal clock, a service-minute log, records requests and meeting briefs (independent advocates on demand at $75 per 30 minutes). When the log shows sustained missed minutes, the parent sees a clearly labeled 'Plan B' in the app: apply their TEFA funds at a clinician-led program running inside a partner accredited school, where the school is school of record and the operating company supplies the clinical director, staff, curriculum, IEP-style compliance, testing and ESA billing. Firewall: advocate income is flat-fee and never tied to placement, and parents get the compensatory-services claim documented before they leave. First sellable products: the Texas parent subscription plus a January 2027 pilot cohort of 8-10 students at one host school.
why_now: TEFA's first year is underway (2026-27) with $1B in funding and 130,000+ applications in the first three weeks. Texas public schools lost about 76,000 students and are closing campuses. Federal special-ed enforcement was hollowed out (OSEP layoffs in Oct 2025, with the office reportedly moving to HHS in June 2026), so parents are actively looking for alternatives and an organized paper trail.
revenue_model: Parent subscriptions at $20 per month, advocate sessions at $75 with a revenue split to a vetted co-op, and per-member fees from parent centers and pediatric groups. Host-program management fee of about 20-25% of ESA revenue per student (about $6-7.5K per $30K student, $60-75K per 10-student program per year), a 15-20% host-school share, plus a $3-5K design fee per host.
non_obvious_insight: A parent's service-minute log is both a legal claim and a qualified lead: it documents exactly who is failing, in which district, for which disability. Aggregated (with consent), the logs form a district-level heat map that tells the operating company where to place the next host program, because demand is proven in the data. One placed student is worth about 25 years of a $20 subscription in a single year, which pays for the tracker's whole acquisition cost, while the tracker's advocate-first brand makes the placement offer credible rather than salesy.
first_30_days: Publish a free Texas IEP clock calculator and letter templates. With admins of 10 state-level special-ed groups, concierge 30 families and measure violations found. List about 150 small accredited private schools in DFW, Houston, San Antonio and Austin and send heads of school a one-page economics sheet. Recruit 10 clinicians. Sign 1-2 pilot hosts for a January 2027 cohort and collect pre-enrollment interest from the 30 concierge families and TEFA parent groups.
lineage: hybrid of I0289 + I1032 (IEP Chief of Staff for Special-Ed Parents + AltSchool Without Buildings: Disability Programs in Host Schools). Why stronger: The tracker's CAC is subsidized by a payer worth an order of magnitude more per family, and the host program gets pre-qualified, motivated, documented leads instead of buying ads. Shared data tells the business where to open programs. Together it is a full lifecycle (enforce, then exit if enforcement fails) that a competitor with only one half cannot offer.
competition_context:
Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: IEP Advocate.ai, ChatGPT and general LLMs (endorsed by CADRE's parent guide), Parent Training and Information Centers (PTIs/CPRCs), Wrightslaw. White space: Confidence is moderate-low. The WebSearch budget hit 200/200 before I could run the planned 6-12 searches, so I found competitors mostly by fetching guessed and known URLs. More direct competitors probably exist that I did not see, and this should be re-run once the search limit is raised.

The core pitch is NOT white space. Deadline extraction, procedural letter generation, meeting prep briefs and state-complaint drafting are already live at IEP Advocate.ai for $30/mo. Free ChatGPT covers much of the rest. A $20/mo 'AI IEP chief of staff' would be a cheaper copy.

Specific gaps I could not find served in the pages I reached:
1. A service-delivery ledger. This means logging minutes promised vs delivered per IEP service line and turning the shortfall into a compensatory-services claim packet. IEP Advocate.ai's fetched pages do not describe service-minute logging or comp-ed calculation.
2. Human-in-the-loop verification. CADRE and K-12 Dive document AI-drafted complaints with fabricated case law and wrong IDEA readings. A product that combines grounded output with vetted advocate or attorney review, at $75 per 30 minutes, is unserved. IEP Advocate.ai has no human tier.
3. B2B2C distribution through parent centers, disability law clinics, pediatric practices and credit unions at $3-6 per member per month. IEP Advocate.ai lists only individual pricing. The channel is unproven.
4. Evidence-grade record keeping. Time-stamped, tamper-evident logs that a hearing officer will accept, rather than chat history. || Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: Fusion Academy (Nord Anglia), Brightmont Academy, Prenda (microschool platform), KaiPod Learning. White space: Research caveat: the WebSearch budget (200 calls) was exhausted before any searches ran, so this verdict rests on about 30 direct page fetches, not the planned 6-12 searches. Google-style discovery of funded startups was not possible, and the negative finding below is unproven. Crunchbase (403), the Comptroller TEFA program pages (404), TEPSAC (503) and several news sites failed.

What the fetches found: no direct competitor was located that runs clinician-led disability programs inside host accredited private schools as the school-of-record structure and bills against TEFA. Adjacent players cover each piece separately.
- Learning-differences schools that build their own campuses: Fusion, Brightmont, Rawson Saunders, Fairhill.
- Microschool platforms: Prenda, KaiPod, Primer.
- Clinician marketplaces: Presence.
- Outside operators embedded in private schools: Catapult.

The unserved wedge is the three-way structure itself. It is a management company that supplies the clinical director, staff, IEP compliance, norm-referenced testing and ESA reconciliation inside a host school. It targets IEP families holding up to $30k accounts in metro Texas in the first TEFA year.

Three risks decide whether the white space is real, and none is resolved:
1. **Legality and accreditor acceptance.** Statute text says a private school must be accredited by a TEPSAC-recognized organization and have continuously operated a campus for at least two school years. It does not address programs within a school or microschools. If the Comptroller, TEA or the accreditor treats a hosted program as a separate campus, or as renting accreditation, the model fails. A 100% pass-through of the ESA to the host with a 20-25% management fee could also draw scrutiny.
2. **Incumbents and hosts.** Existing specialist schools already have eligibility and expertise and may simply expand. Host schools take on IEP compliance liability and reputational risk.
3. **Unit economics.** A 10-student cohort at 20-25% yields $60-75k a year, before clinician cost. Whether that covers a BCBA or dyslexia therapist plus a clinical director was not tested.

title: Credit Bureau for Federal Drug-Refund Receivables
one_liner: Invert lend-and-learn into learn-and-license. A consortium data utility and certified servicer that makes Medicare price-negotiation refunds, later 340B rebates and Part B refunds, a standard scorable collateral class for any lender, wholesaler or credit fund.
customer: First wave is 8-15 specialty lenders, regional banks with pharmacy desks, and family offices or credit funds that already lend to pharmacies or want to. Corporate Capital Direct, ARF, Fora and similar firms, and regional banks, are the named types. Later customers are wholesalers, insurers and note buyers. Pharmacies and hospitals are data suppliers, not customers. They consent because their lender then advances more, faster and cheaper.
problem: Every lender that could fund the refund float meets the same gaps. They cannot verify which claims are MFP-eligible, aged or disputed. They have no dilution history, no controlled payment route and no standard documents. Collateral is invisible to them, so they treat it as ineligible or advance blind at 50-75%. Each lender sees only its own few borrowers, too small a sample to price dilution, so capital does not flow to a float of $500M+ a month. The same gap will repeat in 340B rebate floats (Health Affairs estimates $8.9M-$208M a year per hospital) and in Part B refunds when the 2028 drug cohort arrives.
solution: Product ladder. 1) Within 6 months, the MFP Borrowing-Base Certificate, a portal and API. A lender invites a borrower, the borrower connects a read-only PMS export and the MTF remittance files, and we return a weekly certificate listing eligible refund receivables by claim, age, dilution score, dispute status, recommended reserve and exceptions, with alerts when refunds miss 14- and 21-day marks. 2) The consortium. Anonymized claim-to-refund outcomes from all lenders' borrowers feed a Refund Dilution Index by manufacturer, drug and pharmacy type (median days to pay, reversal and rejection rates), published quarterly. Contributing outcomes is a condition of use, as with credit-bureau furnishing. 3) Standard paper. A master receivables purchase agreement, control-agreement templates and a certified-servicer mark. 4) Later, servicer-of-record and small risk retention on pooled notes sold to insurers and credit funds, and extension to 340B rebate refunds and Part B refunds. Claim data can contain PHI, so we use minimum-necessary fields and business associate agreements from day one.
why_now: The refund class is nine months old and has no standard, no data owner and no legal template. Two expansions are scheduled (semaglutide and 14 more drugs in January 2027, another cohort in 2028). Private credit is hungry for short-duration paper whose obligors are large manufacturers. CMS and HRSA policy keeps shifting, which favors a utility that spans programs over a single-program lender. The MTF remittance and 835 files are standardized, so ingestion is buildable by a small team in months.
revenue_model: Subscription of about $150-$300 a month per monitored borrower, plus about 15-25 bps annualized on certified balances. Index licensing to funds at about $25-100k a year. Later, 30-50 bps servicing on pooled receivables and a 5% retained slice of notes. Illustrative first year: 10 lenders, 600 monitored borrowers and $36M certified is roughly $1.1-1.9M of recurring revenue. The upside is in scale, since each additional program (340B, Part B) reuses the same engine and consortium.
non_obvious_insight: Credit bureaus and ABL field examiners exist because collateral quality is unobservable to lenders. Here it is observable, but only in files that sit in the pharmacy. Whoever collects the first 20 lenders' claim-to-refund outcomes owns the only labeled dataset of statutory-refund dilution, and it compounds, since each new lender lowers every other lender's losses. It also hedges policy risk. If CMS speeds refunds, the index shows it and lenders shift to cheaper advance rates. If not, the float grows and demand rises. The standard travels to other federal refund flows. A single-program lender cannot make that claim.
first_30_days: Build ingestion for the three most common pharmacy management system exports and the MTF remittance files, using files from about 10 pharmacies. Approach 15 lenders and family offices with a free 60-day shadow certificate on three of their existing pharmacy borrowers, in exchange for outcome data and a design-partner letter of intent. Sign 2-3 letters of intent. Put together the borrower consent template and business associate agreement with a healthcare privacy attorney. Sound out one credit fund on eventually buying certified pools.
lineage: mutation of I0499 ('Bridge Loans for Medicare Drug-Price Refunds'), type: 10x-or-inverted
competition_context:
Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: SpendMend (MFP Rebate Reconciliation), Plenful (MFP Intelligence / MFP Command Center), ScriptPro Financial Advantage, Liberty Software (and other PMS vendors, e.g. PioneerRx, PrimeRx, Redsail). White space: Verdict: gap, and a narrow one. In roughly 27 searches across varied terms (MFP refund advance, bridge loan, factoring, fintech, PSAO program, wholesaler program) I found NO product that specifically underwrites and advances against MTF-remitted MFP refunds. Pharmacy lenders sell generic A/R and MCA lines, and the MFP players only sell reconciliation. The unserved space is a claim-level underwriting and servicing capability for refund dilution risk: 340B lesser-of rejections (RARC N907 inappropriate rejections), reversals, Good Faith Inquiry disputes, and authorized-generic refund amounts. It is most valuable for borrowers whose float is large: LTC/senior-care pharmacies, 5-50 store groups, and possibly 340B covered entities in the HRSA rebate pilot, where the float is $8.9M-$208M a year for hospitals (Health Affairs). It also applies to the January 2027 step-up when semaglutide joins.

The wedge is weak in five ways.
1. The 'free missing-refund report' is already crowded: SpendMend, Plenful ($76M raised), ScriptPro, Liberty, and free Beacon MFP dashboards.
2. A typical independent's float is small, about $11k a week or $27k a month per NCPA. At 15-25% APR that is roughly $4-7k a year of gross revenue per pharmacy, before losses and a cost of funds of 8-10%. Customer acquisition through state associations and Facebook groups will be costly relative to that.
3. Wholesalers control the payment path. Cardinal routes MFP refunds through Central Pay and wholesalers auto-debit weekly, so a lender's sweep sits behind the wholesaler in practice. Cardinal customers cannot easily direct refunds to a lender-controlled account.
4. 'Non-recourse' is hard to deliver. Manufacturers can reverse refunds and CMS's own materials describe reversals when claims prove ineligible, so a lender will need pharmacy recourse or holdbacks. That undermines the 'prime paper' insight.
5. Policy is a moving target. CMS made manufacturers include cash-flow mitigation plans in their MFP effectuation plans (accelerated refunds, self-identification). NCPA is still pushing CMS and manufacturers for faster payment, including in Sept 2026 comments on the 2028 guidance.

Adjacent generic lenders can also just add MFP refunds to a borrowing base.

Caveat: the WebSearch budget (200 calls) ran out, so Crunchbase, YC, Product Hunt and open-source sweeps were not fully run. 'No direct competitor found' means not found, not proven absent. | How this version avoids them: SpendMend, Plenful and ScriptPro sell workflow to the pharmacy or health system, and their data is siloed per customer. They are not lender-grade certificates and not a consortium. Beacon and CMS give free dashboards to dispensing entities, not to lenders. Corporate Capital Direct, Live Oak, ARF, Fora and wholesalers become customers instead of competitors, and we never fight for the pharmacy relationship. We can even ingest SpendMend and Plenful outputs as data sources. The main threat is Plenful adding a lender module. The defenses are lender-neutral consortium data that a single vendor cannot replicate, and a certified-servicer standard that lenders can rely on and a wholesaler such as Cardinal cannot credibly be neutral about.

title: Dairy-Backed Calf Guarantee Pool With Immune Screening
one_liner: Invert the parent: instead of selling buyers a verification and later insuring the raiser, make the dairy, who controls colostrum, warrant its own graded calves for 21 days, with our grade as the price of admission and a reserve pool we administer, growing into a mutual or captive with an MGA and reinsurer behind it.
customer: Large dairies (roughly 1,000+ cows, which now sell hundreds to a couple thousand crossbred calves a year, a $0.5-2M line that they still treat as a sideline) that already run good colostrum programs (pasteurized colostrum, Brix testing) and are irritated at being priced at the herd average. First: 3-5 dairies in one region. Second payer: the raisers who pay a premium for guaranteed calves. Later: an insurer or MGA taking over the pool's tail risk.
problem: A dairy with excellent colostrum management cannot credibly say so, so it gets the average price. Buyers cannot underwrite the calves, and insurers cannot underwrite a raiser's loss because the raiser's housing and feeding confound the cause of death (the parent's own moral hazard problem), and federal Livestock Risk Protection excludes mortality and disease. Both sides distrust each other's numbers, and the grade alone still leaves the raiser holding the risk. The dairy owns the biggest early-death driver and holds none of the downside.
solution: Each enrolled dairy has every calf graded at day 3-5 by us. Excellent and Good calves get a Guaranteed tag: if a calf dies of covered causes (neonatal scours, sepsis, weak-calf, navel) within 21 days of delivery, the buyer gets a replacement or price credit up to the lot price. Claims are adjudicated by us using tag custody, necropsy photos or vet note and treatment log within 72 hours. Trauma and raiser-negligence exclusions plus a small buyer co-pay keep the raiser's incentives in play. The dairy pays a per-calf assessment into a segregated reserve we administer, priced by grade and falling as the dairy's grade mix improves, so fixing colostrum is directly rewarded. Poor calves are sold openly at a discount without a guarantee. Unused reserve is rebated at year end, mutual style. Stage 2 (about 50,000 graded calves): a licensed MGA with a fronting carrier and stop-loss reinsurance. Stage 3: a risk retention group or captive owned by participating dairies.
why_now: Beef-on-dairy volume is heading from about 3.2M toward the 5-6M CattleFax projects, at four-figure prices, so a dairy's calf revenue is finally large enough to fund a guarantee and its reputation is worth protecting. A published four-tier standard gives a shared, auditable eligibility rule. Packers already penalize unknown health history and the heifer shortage makes each lost calf expensive to replace, so buyers want risk transfer more than they want a certificate. Cheap custody capture makes claims adjudicable at a few dollars per claim.
revenue_model: $5 per graded calf plus 15-25% administration and commission on guarantee assessments (assessments of about $15-30 per guaranteed calf, in line with an expected covered-loss cost near $15-20 on a $1,200 calf at 1.5% early loss, to be checked against real data), plus profit commission from the reinsurer and float on reserves. Dairy economics: a $35-60 buyer premium against a $15-30 assessment, so about $15-25 net per calf. On 1,000 calves that is a modest but real $15-25K a year. Mature sizing: 500K guaranteed calves a year is about $5M in fees and commissions, with a $10-30M revenue ceiling at 1-2M calves, if the pool becomes the industry standard. The moat is the dataset, the escrow role and the mutual's membership, not the refractometer.
non_obvious_insight: A guarantee is the cheapest credible signal there is (Spence): a seller who will pay if the calf dies proves quality without the buyer trusting any measurement. It also flips the moral hazard. In the first 21 days the risk is controlled by the party paying for it, the dairy, which is why insuring the raiser is hard and warranting the dairy's calves is not. The grade becomes the actuarial rate table rather than a label, and dairies with bad colostrum programs are priced out until they fix them, which turns a data business into a compliance flywheel.
first_30_days: Days 1-14: sign 3-5 large dairies with pasteurized colostrum programs, plus one raiser or broker who will state a premium for guaranteed calves. Draft a one-page 21-day replacement-credit warranty (covered causes, exclusions, 72-hour claim rule, cap at lot price) and get it reviewed by an ag attorney, since a seller's own warranty is a sale-of-goods term but pooling across sellers may be insurance under state law. Open an escrow account. Days 15-30: grade and guarantee a 1,000-calf pilot with each dairy prefunding a $20 per calf reserve. Run the 21-day window and publish the claims ratio. Gates: claims under 80% of assessments and the buyer pays $35 or more a head over the ungraded price. If claims are high, reprice or drop the dairy. Stage 2 only after 50,000 graded calves and a signed MGA term sheet.
lineage: mutation of I0617 ('Immune-Graded Beef-on-Dairy Calves With Warranty'), type: 10x-or-inverted
competition_context:
Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: Where Food Comes From (third-party verification: Age Verification, Source Verification, USDA Process Verified Program, custom Process Verified claims), Calftech Corporation (Central Valley, CA calf ranch). White space: Coverage caveat: the WebSearch budget (200 of 200) was already spent when I started, so I could not run the planned searches on Crunchbase, YC, Product Hunt, TechCrunch or vendor names. The 'nobody does this' finding therefore rests on direct page fetches and a GitHub repository search, not full web coverage. My early attempts to pull search-engine result pages through WebFetch returned junk or CAPTCHAs, and I stopped them because they sidestep the search limit. The verdict is low-to-moderate confidence.

What I found:
- No company selling per-calf independent Brix or serum total protein grading with a QR passport, and no calf-immunity warranty product. Where Food Comes From has no such program. Vytelle's site lists no calf program. GitHub has no relevant open-source tool, only hobby repos.
- Livestock Risk Protection explicitly 'does not protect against mortality, condemnation, physical damage or disease' (https://agproud.com/articles/60060-knowledge-is-the-best-insurance-an-overview-of-livestock-risk-protection). Federal cover for calf death loss is therefore absent. I did not verify what private mortality insurance exists.

What still stands in the way, and is not competition in the strict sense:
1. Self-testing. A raiser can Brix-test at arrival for about $1, and dairies can test their own calves. Independent custody only earns money where seller and buyer distrust each other's numbers, or where price is set before arrival.
2. Bilateral history. Feeders already ask which dairy the calves came from and some supply sire straws to dairies (https://agproud.com/articles/53106-factors-to-consider-before-buying-crossbred-dairy-beef-calves). Source-dairy reputation substitutes for per-calf grading.
3. Warranty moral hazard. Immunity is one driver of loss, but raiser housing, feeding and biosecurity dominate, which makes underwriting hard. Lombard's consensus paper puts failure of passive transfer at roughly twice the risk, which is a useful signal but not a full loss model.
4. Incumbents can absorb it. Verifiers, diagnostics vendors, calf-ranch networks and packer programs could add an immunity field.

Genuinely unserved: an independent, per-calf immunity record that travels from dairy to raiser to feeder to packer, plus a neutral dispute-resolution measurement. | How this version avoids them: Where Food Comes From is a verifier and does not take underwriting positions or hold per-calf outcome data, so it can be a claims-audit partner rather than a rival. Calftech-style integrated ranches earn credibility by owning both ends and keeping data in-house. This gives any dairy the same credibility without owning a ranch, as a capital-light replica of vertical integration, and integrated operators simply become additional buyers of guaranteed calves. The parent's stated obstacles are answered directly. Self-testing is irrelevant because the guarantee, not the number, carries the trust. Bilateral history is replaced by a financial commitment. Warranty moral hazard is contained by a short window on dairy-controlled causes, exclusions and a co-pay. No federal mortality cover exists (LRP excludes it), and I could not verify what private livestock mortality insurance exists, so the plan partners with an MGA instead of competing with one.

title: AI Chat-History Exposure Assessments for Breach Counsel
one_liner: When infostealers grab employees' AI sessions, tell breach counsel what the attacker could actually have read and whether notification is triggered.
customer: Incident-response boutiques, privacy and breach law firms, cyber-insurer panel vendors, and enterprise DPOs. Priced per incident.
problem: Infostealer logs exposed AI sessions tied to 80,000+ corporate domains, and 358 of 482 large companies analyzed had stolen ChatGPT/OpenAI sessions. A stolen session is a searchable archive of contracts, source code, and personal data, and it bypasses MFA. IR tooling was built for mailboxes and file shares, so nobody can say whether an AI-history breach triggers legal notification.
solution: Ingest infostealer-feed hits mapped to employee AI accounts. Combine them with the customer's enterprise export or compliance-API data to classify the sampled chats after the theft window by data class (PII, PHI, credentials, deal information, source code). Deliver a notification-decision memo, an affected-person list, remediation steps (session revocation, key rotation), and an insurer-ready timeline.
why_now: The 2026 infostealer data shows stolen AI sessions at scale. Enterprise AI adoption now puts sensitive work in chat, and insurers are adding AI exclusions, so they want scoping evidence before paying.
revenue_model: $5-25K per incident, with $1-2K per month monitoring retainers and channel referral fees.
non_obvious_insight: The breach is not the stolen cookie but the content behind it, and notification law turns on data, not credentials. No tool in the IR stack handles AI transcripts, so a small team can own the category before platform vendors bother.
first_30_days: Sign 3 IR boutiques as channel partners. Build a classification pipeline over enterprise chat exports. Run the first paid assessments at a $7.5K flat fee using hits from commercial infostealer-intel feeds.
lineage: original (tournament survivor)
competition_context:
Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: Hudson Rock (Cavalier, infostealers.com, CavalierGPT), SpyCloud, Flare, Constella Intelligence. White space: Across the pages I could fetch, no vendor sells the specific deliverable: a counsel-facing 'what could the attacker have read, and does notification trigger' determination for a stolen AI session. The gap sits between three groups. Infostealer-intel vendors (Hudson Rock, SpyCloud, Flare, Constella) detect the stolen session but stop there. AI-DLP and DSPM vendors (Varonis, Cyera, Harmonic, Cyberhaven, Reco, Purview) classify current or real-time chat data for the customer's own governance. Breach-review platforms (Relativity and IR firms) build notification lists but show no ingestion of AI chat transcripts. What remains open is the forensic and legal bridge: joining the theft window from the feed with provider-side session-access evidence and the chat content, then producing a privilege-friendly memo and affected-person list.

Caveats on the wedge:
- The WebSearch budget ran out, so I could not check funded startups, Product Hunt, YC or open-source projects. A stealth startup is possible.
- I could not verify the '358 of 482' or '80,000 domains' figures.
- The wedge depends on data access. A theft of a personal or free-tier account leaves the employer with no export. Only Enterprise and Edu tenants have admin export or Compliance API data, and I could not confirm the current API terms because the OpenAI help pages returned 403.
- A stolen cookie in a feed does not prove the attacker viewed the chats, so the assessment depends on provider audit logs that only OpenAI or the tenant admin can see.
- Any vendor holding the customer's chat data (Cyera, Varonis, Purview) can add this as a services line quickly.

title: The True Acceptance Map for Rural Transfers
one_liner: Voice AI agents call every receiving psychiatric unit and specialty hospital each night to learn what they will actually accept, and rural ERs text a number to find out who will say yes.
customer: Critical access hospital EDs, state hospital associations and state rural health offices (paid with Rural Health Transformation Program funds), and state behavioral health authorities. Subscription per hospital or per state.
problem: A rural ER holding a suicidal 16-year-old, or a stroke, trauma or OB patient, may spend 3-8 hours making phone calls to place them. State bed registries say beds are open, but the real decision is made by a house supervisor at 2am applying unwritten rules: no IV drug history, no one-to-one sitter, no autism, no patients over 250 lb, no out-of-state Medicaid, no aggression, and no calls after 9pm without a physician-to-physician call. Every ER charge nurse keeps a battered binder or a phone note of who says yes to what and who to ask for. It lives in one head, and it goes out of date when a house supervisor changes.
solution: Use voice agents to call each facility's intake line on a schedule and extract structured, current answers: true open capacity by population, unwritten exclusions, insurance rules, the name and direct number of the person who decides, and the hours that person answers. Serve it back through a plain SMS interface. A nurse texts 'psych, 16yo, Medicaid, sitter needed, hx cutting' and gets a ranked call list with the exact script to use (the words that get an acceptance). Only facility rules are collected. No patient data is ever in the calls. Later, sell a receiving-side listing so facilities can pre-qualify referrals and get fewer dead-end calls.
why_now: Every state has now posted Rural Health Transformation Program funding opportunities (as of August 2026), and care coordination and access technology are core uses. Research on bed-tracking systems shows registries still leave clinicians phoning to check appropriateness, especially for aggressive, medically complex, autistic and dementia patients. Voice agents from 2025-26 can now hold a natural two-minute call with an intake nurse for a few cents. The workforce shortage means intake lines are answered by fewer people, which makes the tacit rules more valuable.
revenue_model: $300-600 per ER per month for SMS access. State-level licenses of $100-300k per year paid from RHTP or behavioral health funds. A second line is a receiving-facility listing at about $500 per month per facility. The proprietary asset is a data graph of real rules that no registry has.
non_obvious_insight: The valuable data is not bed counts, which are wrong within an hour. It is the tacit acceptance criteria and the identity of the human who decides, and it can only be learned by phone at night. That is why bed-registry vendors (built on hospital self-reporting) miss it. Wire an off-the-shelf voice agent platform to call each facility nightly and write results to a table. Put an SMS bot in front of it with a Twilio number. Give it free to five ERs in the region and compare call counts and time to placement before and after. Bring the numbers to the state hospital association and the RHTP office.

title: Private Road Associations in a Box
one_liner: Turn the neighbors' informal, cash-in-a-coffee-can road fund into a recorded, insurable road association with dues, reserves and competitively bid plowing and grading.
customer: Households on private roads and shared driveways (5-60 homes per road). The urgent buyers are the real estate attorneys, title agents and listing agents whose closings stall without an enforceable road maintenance agreement.
problem: Millions of rural households reach their homes by private roads maintained by handshake. One neighbor plows, some chip in, some free-ride. Washouts and disputes are common. Lenders and title insurers often want a recorded, enforceable maintenance agreement, so sales stall. HOA software assumes an incorporated HOA with a manager, not 12 neighbors and a gravel road.
solution: Fixed-fee formation: map who benefits, draft a state-specific maintenance agreement, record it with the county, and set up a simple legal entity or association where state law allows. Then recurring service: ACH dues collection with reminders and lien-based enforcement where allowed, a reserve fund, standing bids from vetted plow, gravel and grading contractors, a photo log of road condition, and storm-damage documentation packages for county or FEMA requests.
why_now: Post-2020 in-migration put many remote workers on rural private roads. Extreme-weather washouts, such as Hurricane Helene's damage to private roads and bridges in western North Carolina in 2024, showed how many neighborhoods have no entity that can pool money or apply for repair aid. Lenders and insurers keep tightening property-access checks. No vertical software serves informal neighbor groups.
revenue_model: $1,500-3,000 formation fee, paid by the neighborhood or by the seller at closing. $12-25 per household per month for dues administration. A disclosed 5-8% procurement fee on managed contractor bids.
non_obvious_insight: The customer with urgency isn't the neighborhood but the closing. A failed sale costs a seller and an agent five figures, so attorneys and agents will send you deals for a flat fee. Recurring revenue then comes from dues float and admin. At 200 associations you are the largest single buyer of plowing and gravel in a region, which gives you procurement leverage no individual road has.
first_30_days: Pick a state dense with private roads (Maine, Vermont, New Hampshire, or the North Carolina mountains). Get an attorney to draft a reusable agreement template. Partner with 3-5 real estate attorneys and title agents who see failed closings. Sell a $1,500 'closing rescue' formation package. Run 2 pilot associations with free dues collection for 6 months to prove the workflow.
lineage: original (tournament survivor)
competition_context:
Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: PayHOA, Mainstream HOA and community-association platforms (Buildium, AppFolio, FrontSteps, Vantaca, CINC and similar), DIY legal templates and local real estate attorneys (Nolo, US Legal Forms, LegalZoom-style forms, local attorney drafting), Public alternatives: state road-association statutes and county road or special-assessment districts. White space: Tentative. Coverage was thin, so absence of a dedicated venture-backed product is not proven. What I found unserved:
1. No product I could find bundles the closing-triggered legal package (state-specific maintenance agreement, county recording, a lightweight entity) with the ongoing administration for informal neighbor groups. PayHOA covers dues admin generically and cheaply; the statutes and the law-firm and forms market cover formation; nobody stitches them together for the 5-60 home private road.
2. Competitively bid, pooled procurement of plowing and gravel across many associations. I found no tool for it.
3. Storm-damage documentation and an organized entity ready for state or FEMA private-road aid. NC's program required a single point of contact, ownership proof and a 50% HOA cost share, so unorganized roads were poorly placed to claim.
4. The transaction-channel distribution (attorneys, title agents and listing agents at a stalled closing) looks unowned by software vendors.

Weak points:
- The recurring $12-25 per household per month is 6-12 times PayHOA's roughly $2 per household.
- Lien-based enforcement is state-dependent. NC's G.S. 136-102.6 only requires disclosure of who maintains private streets, and my Maine excerpt covered assessment authority but not liens.
- Holding dues float triggers trust-accounting and money-handling rules.
- The 5-8% procurement fee creates a conflict of interest.

title: Megawatt Credit Bureau with Bonded Collateral
one_liner: Invert the vetting desk: real developers pay to be rated, utilities accept the rating for lower deposits, and the company eventually underwrites large-load security bonds off the physical-readiness data, so regulators' collateral rules become the market instead of the threat.
customer: First payer: mid-size and regional developers with real sites and real equipment slots (powered-land developers, ex-bitcoin-miner sites converting to AI, regional colo builders) that are in 10-30 utility queues and being asked for $50K/MW collateral or up to $100K per study in each. Accepting side: co-op and municipal pools that agree to recognize the rating. Capital side: a specialty surety or insurance carrier and reinsurer that provide bond capacity through an MGA structure.
problem: Collateral regimes (Texas proposes $50K/MW, AEP Ohio-style deposits) treat every applicant as a phantom. A real 300 MW project must lock up $15M in cash or letters of credit per utility, and re-submit the same package to each co-op. Hyperscaler-backed developers have the balance sheet and shells do not, so thinly capitalized developers with real projects get squeezed or forced to sell to bigger players. Surety and LC markets price the principal's balance sheet, not the project's physical readiness, so there is no credit signal between a hyperscaler guarantee and a shell LLC. Utilities cannot tell the difference either.
solution: Phase 1 (months 0-6): the 'Verified Ready' dossier for $15-25K. The developer hands over what real projects have (air permit, deed or option, OEM slot confirmation, EPC contract, tenant LOI, financing letter), and the desk verifies it through public records and direct confirmation calls. It issues a dated, registry-anchored readiness rating (R1-R5) that pilot co-op pools accept as satisfying Gates 0-1 and as grounds for a 30-50% deposit reduction or study priority. Utilities pay nothing. Phase 2 (months 6-18): a bonded-collateral program, meaning surety-style 'large-load security bonds' written by a specialty carrier through an MGA, priced off the rating and posted to the utility as obligee in place of part of the cash or LC collateral. Phase 3: publish the methodology as an open standard and lobby tariffs and regulators to reference it, e.g. 'rated applicants may post bonds or reduced collateral.' The registry accumulates milestone-hit data on who actually energizes, which becomes proprietary loss data no one else has.
why_now: Texas SB 6 (final rule due by 12/31/2026), AEP Ohio-style minimum-demand tariffs and study fees of up to $100K created a huge new collateral requirement that did not exist 18 months ago, and each dollar of required cash collateral creates demand for a cheaper substitute. Transformer lead times of 3-5 years and switchgear sold out into 2028 make equipment evidence a cheap, hard-to-fake readiness signal that a rating can be built on. Roughly half of announced 2026 builds are delayed or canceled, so utilities and lenders are hunting for a credible signal.
revenue_model: Rating fee $15-25K (up to $75K per GW) per developer per accepting utility set, plus $5K/yr renewals. Bond premium of 2-3% a year on the security amount, with the MGA taking about 20-25% commission plus profit share and the carrier taking the risk. Later, registry data licences to lenders and utilities. Illustrative: 40 rated projects in year 1 is about $800K. At 100 bonded projects a year with $15M average security, that is $1.5B of security, about $37M of premium and about $9M of MGA revenue. It rises further if regulators adopt the rating in tariffs.
non_obvious_insight: Regulators' collateral rules look like the death of a vetting business, but they are the birth of a substitute market, and a substitute needs an underwriter that can price physical readiness. The paying base self-selects to real projects because phantoms will not pay to be scrutinized. The classic conflict of interest of issuer-paid ratings is solved by having the MGA and carrier carry loss exposure, so the rater has skin in the game, unlike a ratings shop. Finally, the segment nobody serves is the thin-balance-sheet developer with real equipment slots, whose risk is legible only in the logistics trail. The rating therefore turns a compliance cost into a moat: loss data on who energizes.
first_30_days: Days 1-10: interview 15 mid-size developers, sourced from the 384 developers on Cleanview's tracker, powered-land brokers and LinkedIn, asking how many co-op queues they are in, how much collateral is posted and how many times they have re-submitted. Days 10-20: pre-sell 3 dossiers at a $10K founding price, refundable if no co-op accepts. Use the free co-op back-test as the lead magnet to sign an MOU with one G&T pool to accept the dossier for deposit relief. Draft methodology v0.1 and publish it openly. Days 20-30: talk to 2 commercial surety brokers or MGAs that already place utility deposit bonds and get term-sheet-level interest, not a binder. Deliver the first dossier. Kill test: if no G&T will trade a rating for lower deposits, the utility-acceptance leg fails and the bond phase never starts.
lineage: mutation of I0079 ('Phantom Load Vetting Desk for Rural Utilities'), type: 10x-or-inverted
competition_context:
Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: GridUnity, Clean Power Research (PowerClerk), Enverus, LandGate. White space: I found no direct competitor. No startup, consultancy or association was selling a utility-side, per-inquiry 'is this developer physically real' memo with a recommended collateral amount and milestone-gated study structure. The gap is real but narrow.

What is unserved: (1) External physical-trail verification for small utilities, meaning air-permit generator counts vs claimed MW, recorded deeds and options, LLC principal cross-checks, and OEM or EPC evidence. GridUnity and PowerClerk track applicant-supplied data but do not verify it. Enverus, LandGate and GridCARE serve the developer side. (2) A cross-utility duplicate-request registry. Texas SB 6 mandates duplicate-request disclosure only inside ERCOT. Outside ERCOT there is no pooled registry. Developers do file the same project with several utilities (Latitude Media, Utility Dive). (3) Packaging for 5-person co-op engineering staffs: I found no NRECA vetting checklist or tool, and no small-utility-specific vendor.

Serious weaknesses the founder must address:
- Regulation and tariffs are substituting for vetting. Collateral, study fees and site-control mandates make the applicant self-prove. Exelon cut its estimates about 40% after stricter collateral. AEP Ohio's pipeline fell by more than half after study fees of up to $100K (https://techstartups.com/2026/09/01/ai-data-centers-request-700-gw-of-u-s-power-but-much-of-the-demand-may-be-an-illusion/). Once a co-op requires a deposit, site control and a signed LOI, much of the 12-point test becomes documents the applicant hands over.
- Texas SB 6 / 16 TAC 25.194 applies only in ERCOT (https://www.dlapiper.com/en-us/insights/publications/2026/03/texas-proposes-new-interconnection-standards-for-large-electric-loads). The 'small utilities in neighboring states get the displaced phantoms' claim is plausible but I found no evidence for it.
- Several tests may not be observable by an outsider. OEM order acknowledgments and financing letters are confidential, and real developers often approach the utility before ordering equipment.
- Regulators are absorbing the LLC-transparency piece. Texas ordered an audit requiring true-ownership disclosure, and Pennsylvania issued an August 18 executive order for projects over 25 MW.
- Big engineering consultancies could add this as a service line. I could not verify whether they already do. My web-search budget ran out before I could check. | How this version avoids them: GridUnity and PowerClerk are utility workflow tools, and the rating is a credential they can ingest. Enverus, LandGate and GridCARE help developers pick sites or find capacity but do not verify readiness or produce a rating a utility will accept for lower deposits. Cleanview is a public tracker with no verification or credential. ZEG is advisory consulting. NRECA is a distribution channel that can endorse the standard but cannot underwrite. A two-sided credential (developers pay, utilities accept) that later carries insurance-backed loss data has network and data economics none of them touch, and the parent's own problem, that collateral rules substitute for vetting, is turned into the demand driver.

title: Plug-or-Pitch: Turning Idle Wells Into Assets
one_liner: Screen idle and orphan oil wells for hydrogen, helium and heat evidence, and get paid a share of the plugging liability that disappears when a well is transferred to an explorer who wants a ready-made hole to the basement.
customer: The payer is the liability holder, not the explorer. Wedge: independent operators in Kansas and Oklahoma holding 50-500 idle, shut-in or temporarily abandoned wells under rising plugging and bonding pressure. Phase 2: state orphan-well programs (funded by the $4.7B IIJA orphan-well money) and state land offices. The other side of the transaction, who takes the well and pays a placement fee, is a hydrogen, helium or geothermal junior that today drills new holes at seven-figure cost.
problem: An idle well is a negative asset: plugging often costs tens of thousands of dollars per well (an estimate to confirm state by state), and operators or states carry that liability for years. Meanwhile the parent idea's buyers spend roughly seven figures to drill a test hole to basement, and a wellbore that already penetrates basement, with a file that shows non-flammable gas or elevated temperature, is worth many multiples of its plugging cost to them. The two sides never find each other because the evidence sits in scanned well files, and juniors in the parent's research 'do not budget $15-50k a year for data' but do budget hard money for holes. Price anchored to a known plugging cost is a much easier sale than price anchored to speculative exploration value.
solution: A per-well 'Reuse Dossier' built from each idle well's own file and its offsets: hydrogen/helium/N2-rich gas shows from mud logs, DSTs and driller notes, depth to basement, casing/cement/plugging status, bottom-hole temperature and gradient, and produced-water chemistry, each with page-image provenance and a confidence grade. A Reuse Score estimates re-entry cost against new-drill cost and states the single test that would confirm the lead. Wells are bundled into small re-entry lots and placed with repurposers under a recorded assignment of plugging liability (with state transfer approval and financial assurance), often keeping a retained royalty or carry for the seller. The operator pays nothing upfront: screening is free and the startup is paid from the avoided liability and from the placement. Geothermal scoring can be sourced from partners such as WellScout AI rather than built.
why_now: State and federal pressure on idle wells is at its peak: IIJA orphan-well plugging money is flowing through the late 2020s, and states have built lists that did not exist five years ago. Hydrogen and helium juniors raised $20M-$245M rounds (Koloma, Terra AI, Mantle8) and HyTerra proved that twinning historic wells works, so demand for cheap access to basement-penetrating holes is real. VLM extraction cost per well file has collapsed to a few dollars, which makes free screening for an operator affordable on a contingency basis; that would have been uneconomic in 2022.
revenue_model: Contingent success fee of about 15% of the avoided plugging cost (from the operator or state) when a well transfers, plus a $10-25k placement fee (or 5% of any bonus or sale price) from the repurposer, plus $500-1,500 for a premium dossier and a $10-25k/year 'reuse lot' feed for juniors. Illustrative unit economics: an operator with 200 idle wells costs about $16k to screen (about $80/well compute plus geologist review); if 1-2% clear the bar (1-2 wells above the 0.5% Paris Basin rate is plausible for a targeted fairway) and each saves about $40k of plugging cost, revenue is $6-12k in liability fees plus placement fees per portfolio, and a state program is 10-50x that. The wedge is deliberately contingent so the customer has no downside.
non_obvious_insight: The bid-ask spread has the wrong sign: the holder sees a negative asset (minus the plugging cost) and the explorer sees a hole worth a multiple of its plugging cost, and the only missing ingredient is verified evidence about which wells sit on the positive side. Low hit rate (about 0.5% in the Paris Basin study) kills a subscription atlas but not a contingency screen, because the operator's cost is zero and one hit pays for the portfolio. The startup's true asset is not the data but the transferable, state-approved playbook for liability assignment plus a book of buyers, which creates a two-sided market that data vendors and free datasets cannot replicate.
first_30_days: Week 1: pull the public inactive/TA well lists from the Kansas KCC and Oklahoma OCC and pick 300 wells that reach basement in the Nemaha corridor. Week 2: extract their files and offsets and produce 30 Reuse Dossiers with a scored top 10. Week 3: call 25 independent operators and the plugging-fund manager at one state agency with the offer 'give us your 100 worst idle wells, screening is free, we take 15% of the avoided plugging cost if we place a well'. In parallel get 2-3 juniors to sign non-binding LOIs to consider re-entry lots. Week 4: sign 3 contingency agreements and confirm with the state regulator what transfer-with-assumption of liability requires. Before building further, run 15 calls to check the two unverified assumptions: state transfer rules and re-entry cost versus a new drill.
lineage: mutation of I1085 ('Dry-Hole Atlas for Hydrogen, Helium, Geothermal'), type: new-customer-or-model
competition_context: Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: USGS/BLM Natural Gas Compositional Analyses Dataset (free), USGS Geologic Hydrogen Prospectivity Map Explorer, SMU / NGDS heat-flow and corrected bottom-hole-temperature database (now on the DOE Geothermal Data Repository), Project InnerSpace GeoMap. White space: The wedge that remains is narrow but real. Nobody found sells page-level, provenance-linked hydrogen, helium and heat evidence extracted from the unstructured parts of old well files. That means mud-log gas shows, drill-stem-test and production-test reports, driller notes such as non-flammable gas, and water-well gas, all at lease-block or section level. The free datasets (USGS/BLM, SMU/GDR, KGS) already cover the structured gas-analysis and corrected-BHT layers, so a paid product cannot rest on those. The USGS roughly 16,000 He-bearing points and the 30,000 corrected BHT wells are a free baseline that any paid product has to beat. Koloma, Zanskar, HyTerra and MAX Power already do this in-house, so the addressable buyers are the smaller players (AKAP counts 123 companies in natural hydrogen, Rystad counted 40) plus the lease and land side. | How this version avoids them: USGS/BLM, KGS, SMU/GDR and GeoMap: free datasets give regional or aggregate layers, none identifies which specific idle well is a transferable reuse candidate, so they are our inputs, not substitutes. WellScout AI is the closest overlap (screens oil wells for geothermal conversion); it covers only heat and sells software to operators, so we can partner on thermal scoring and win on multi-commodity gas evidence plus the transaction. Koloma, HyTerra, MAX Power, Zanskar keep their data in-house and are demand-side buyers of re-entry lots, not rivals. NthDS and Enverus/TGS sell files to buyers of O&G data; they do not take contingent fees on liability transfers and have channel conflict doing so. title: Serial Match: AP-Only Recovery for Exchange Buyers
one_liner: A success-fee audit that takes one accounts-payable export from an independent rotable pool or Part 145 station, finds money its repair vendors already owe, and collects it. It starts with credits the vendor has already conceded, then moves to repeat-failure claims.
customer: Independent rotable exchange pools, parts resellers and Part 145 stations that buy a few hundred outsourced repairs and exchange units a year from 10 or more shops, roughly $5-40M of repair spend (my assumption, unverified). The buyer is the Controller or VP Materials at a firm with a 2-4 person back office. These firms sit outside power-by-the-hour contracts, so the warranty exposure is theirs. They multi-source on price, so they have little vendor-relationship fear. They also see the same serial number pass through many hands. Regionals, EMS operators and lessors are phase 2.
problem: The parent idea had four named weaknesses: PBH and maintenance-plan contracts remove warranty exposure for many small fleets, integrating with each operator's maintenance system is hard, fear of annoying the shop, and no proof anyone pays. A pool has none of these. Its serialized units cycle through repair invoices, exchange credits and core returns. The same P/N and S/N can appear on two invoices from one shop within the warranty window, and nobody joins invoice lines by serial number. Beside that sit credit memos issued but never applied, core credits not netted, no-fault-found evaluation fees on in-warranty units, and turnaround guarantees never credited. Pool gross margins are thin, so recovering 1-3% of repair spend moves EBITDA. The warranty windows are short and full of exclusions, so recovery has to be systematic, with a claim filed for every eligible unit.
solution: Input is one vendor-ledger export plus the invoice PDFs, with no maintenance-system integration. An LLM extractor builds a serial-level table: P/N (including interchangeable P/Ns), S/N, repair date, charges and the warranty text printed on the invoice or PO. Recovery runs in three passes, ordered from least to most disputed. Pass 1 is zero-dispute money: open and unapplied credit memos, duplicate payments, and core credits not applied. Pass 2 is the repeat-serial detector: the same S/N back to the same shop inside its window, plus the same S/N failing after different shops' repairs. Pass 3 is contested items: NFF fees on in-warranty units and turnaround-guarantee credits. Claims go out on each vendor's own form. A vendor playbook library covers the top 60 shops: warranty terms, exclusions, contacts, average days to credit and past acceptance rate. We chase every claim to a posted credit or cash. Phase 2 adds read-only receiving and removal data from the customer's ERP to confirm failures the invoices alone can't show.
why_now: Reliable, cheap LLM extraction from messy repair-invoice PDFs and warranty fine print is what makes an AP-only audit viable. Before 2025 it needed offshore data-entry teams, which killed contingency margins. Aftermarket parts prices and repair turn times have also climbed since the 2022-23 supply squeeze (my assumption, unverified). That makes each exchange unit worth more, so pools tie up more capital in them and each unclaimed failure costs more.
revenue_model: Contingency fee of 20% of cash and credits recovered, or 25% on contested pass-3 items, with a 12-month tail after the audit. The fee is due only when cash arrives or the credit is applied, not when the memo is issued. That solves the objection to paying cash on a credit the customer can only spend at that shop. There is no upfront cost and no minimum. Year 2 adds a $2-4k/month continuous-monitoring tier for pools with over $15M of spend. Anonymized vendor-acceptance and turn-time data is a later product.
non_obvious_insight: Sequence matters more than segment. Leading with credits the vendor has already conceded gives first cash in 3-4 weeks, with no dispute and no relationship risk. That builds the trust to file contested claims later. Every contested claim, won or lost, adds to the playbook library: per-shop acceptance rates, exclusion language and time to credit. That library is the cornered resource and process power a generalist cannot copy. The pool is also the freight-audit shipper of aviation: high invoice volume, many vendors, serial-tracked goods and no reason to protect any single vendor.
first_30_days: Build a target list of about 60 pools and Part 145 stations from public repair-station and trade-association directories. Send 40 direct outreach messages offering a free scan: they send 12 months of vendor ledger and invoices, and we return the dollars found within 10 business days. The only thing we ask for is permission to file. Hire a retired warranty or materials coordinator as a paid advisor for vendor quirks. Close 3 audits and deliver ranked claim lists. File pass-1 claims first and aim for the first credit memo by day 30. Set an explicit kill test: if the median first-pass yield is under 1% of repair spend across the first 5 files, stop or narrow the segment. Publish the aggregate finding, such as the share of eligible repeat repairs never claimed, as the lead magnet.

title: Well Covenant Trustee for Rural Data Center Counties
one_liner: A neutral program administrator writes, monitors and runs a county-mandated, developer-funded private-well protection covenant, where excess drawdown versus upgradient control wells triggers in-kind remediation with no lawsuit and no sensor sales.
customer: Wedge: county attorneys and planning directors in rural, private-well counties that are already drafting developer-funded monitoring and neighbor-escrow language (Franklin County IN draft v3.0, Shenandoah County VA, and similar counties in GA, PA and IN). Payer: the independent developer of a 50-500 MW campus in that county, which funds the covenant because the county makes it a permit or development-agreement condition. Not hyperscalers with in-house community teams.
problem: Dry or silted wells are what actually produce lawsuits and hearing revolts (Meta / Newton County GA: neighbors say wells went dry, Meta's own study says groundwater flows away, families sued in Sept 2026). Nobody can separate data-center drawdown from drought or other pumping, so developer-commissioned studies are not believed and neighbor claims cannot be proven. Counties are drafting escrow and monitoring language from scratch, with no tested trigger, no neutral administrator and no legal structure. The parent's sensor-baseline product is a crowded, commoditizing layer (KETOS, Aethair, Envirosuite, consultancies), and its automatic cash payout risks being classed as insurance or read as an admission of liability.
solution: Sell trusteeship of a well covenant, not sensors. (1) A paste-in Covenant Kit for county attorneys: development-agreement rider, trust instrument, enrollment rules, and a published trigger protocol. (2) Trigger design: 8-12 upgradient control wells outside the cone of influence, a 12-month pre-construction regression of each enrolled household well on the control wells, and the developer's metered pumping records shared with the panel. A trigger fires only on sustained deviation beyond the control-adjusted trend (for example >5 ft and >2 standard errors for 30 days), so the developer pays for excess drawdown and not for drought. (3) Remedy is in kind, not cash indemnity: emergency water hauling in 24-48 hours, then pump lowering or well deepening by a pre-qualified local driller at a fixed rate card. The developer is the obligor and a corporate trustee (a regional bank trust department) holds the escrow. We are administrator and data steward and never hold the money. That structure is closer to a remediation trust or warranty than to an insurance policy, and a counsel opinion is the gate. (4) Governance: a 3-person technical panel with one member appointed by the county (ideally from state extension or the geological survey), one by the developer and one by a residents' council. (5) Hardware and labs are bought from KETOS, Eno Scientific, Kunak-type vendors. Noise, PM2.5 and voltage are paid add-ons later.
why_now: Permit politics moved to governors in 2026 (NY Executive Order 62 on July 14, Texas TCEQ permit halt on Sept 21), and counties are writing the rules now. Franklin County's draft already contains developer-paid monitoring wells, a licensed-hydrogeologist assessment and an escrow for 24-hour potable water to impacted neighbors. Shenandoah County officials back applicant-funded third-party testing, and St. Louis's permit requires a developer-funded hydraulic study. Ordinances get copied county to county, so a ready, legally vetted kit written this quarter can become the template. The Newton County lawsuit (Sept 2026) shows what a baseline-less well dispute costs.
revenue_model: Paid by the developer through the county-mandated covenant. Illustrative program of 500 enrolled households: $1,000 per household setup (mostly hardware pass-through, about 25% margin) = $500k; $480 per household per year for telemetry, QA, lab checks and reporting = $240k per year at about 55% gross margin; administrator fee of 1% per year on a $1.5M remediation reserve (about $2,500 per household) = $15k; $500 per adjudicated claim. Extensions add per-household noise, air and voltage modules. Later: license the trigger protocol and dataset to state agencies and insurers. Assumptions to test: expected remedy claim rate of 5-10% of wells over 10 years, and $8-15k per remedy.
non_obvious_insight: The real buyer is the county attorney, not the developer. Because the county imposes the covenant, the developer's objection to volunteering a payout (an implied admission) disappears, and the county gets an instrument it cannot write itself. The economics are also better for developers than the alternative: NorthPoint offered $10k to each of 4,500 households ($45M) and was accused of bribery, while an in-kind covenant reserve for the households that could plausibly lose water is a small fraction of that and is credible because a neutral panel decides. Attribution is fixed in the design (control wells and pumping records), not argued afterward.
first_30_days: Days 1-7: get Franklin County IN's draft v3.0 and the Shenandoah County notes, call the county attorneys and planning directors, and offer to draft the covenant and trust instrument free in exchange for being named in the draft. Days 10-30: run the parent's 10-neighbor-well pilot in a county with a pending hearing, but with control wells and the regression trigger back-tested on 12 months of public USGS or state well data, and bring the term sheet plus live dashboard to the hearing. Kill gate at 90 days: one developer or county puts a funded escrow in writing and counsel signs off; otherwise stop.

title: Warranty Gap Desk for MEP Contractors
one_liner: Sell to the electrical and mechanical contractors who promise owners a warranty from substantial completion while their OEM warranties run from shipment or startup, and fund the service from the contractors' own warranty reserves.
customer: The warranty manager, contracts VP or CFO at mid-size to large electrical contractors, mechanical contractors and construction managers building data centers who furnish the MEP equipment themselves (colo, enterprise and neocloud jobs, not owner-furnished hyperscale). They give the owner a 12-24 month warranty and carry a warranty reserve on the balance sheet.
problem: The parent assumed the owner feels the pain. The party actually squeezed between two clocks is the contractor. The OEM warranty passes through on an OEM calendar (startup or 18 months from ship). The contractor's promise to the owner runs from substantial completion or Tier certification, and owner-side counsel are actively advising developers to push warranty commencement to certification (the law-firm guidance in the parent's evidence). Every month of delay widens the gap, and in that gap the contractor pays for defects out of pocket. Estimators price it as a flat percentage, project managers do not track it, and closeout binders bury the OEM terms. Contractor warranty reserves are real P&L items the CFO wants released, which gives a budget line the parent never had.
solution: 1) Bid-stage gap pricing. Read the subcontract warranty clause and the OEM quotes, compute gap-days by equipment line, and price it into the bid instead of a flat reserve. 2) Deferral riders on the contractor's own POs. A contractor buying hundreds of units per year has leverage the owner lacks, and the desk pools rider purchasing across contractor clients for discounts. 3) Pre-expiry proof test and claim filing on installed gear so the OEM, not the contractor, pays for defects (load-bank partner does the physical work). 4) Reserve-release package at contract end: a documented file showing what OEM claims were accepted and what exposure remains, so the CFO can release reserve early.
why_now: Owner counsel now push warranty starts to Tier certification while long-lead delivery and phase slippage stretch the shipment-to-certification interval. Data center MEP backlogs are large, so contractors have more warranty exposure on more sites than ever. Extraction of PO, contract and OEM terms into gap-days used to require a warranty analyst per job and is now nearly free.
revenue_model: Program fee per project, roughly 0.03-0.08% of MEP contract value (about $120-320K on a $400M scope), which is a small share of a typical reserve. Assumption to validate: reserves of around 0.5-2% of contract value. Plus 20% of OEM-accepted claims that would otherwise have been borne by the contractor. Plus a rider-pooling margin or referral fee from OEMs and rental partners. Renewals follow the contractor's project pipeline, so revenue is recurring across projects.
non_obvious_insight: The contractor is the only party in the chain holding an unhedged, quantifiable, budgeted warranty liability, and it is growing because of owner-side contract trends. Selling to the contractor also flips the leverage problem: one contractor buys from OEMs at volume, and a desk representing several contractors can win start-date deferrals that no single owner could. The buyer is a CFO with a reserve, not an owner's ops team with no budget.
first_30_days: Call 15 warranty managers and project executives at regional electrical and mechanical contractors with live data center work, sourced through NECA and MCAA chapters and surety brokers who track contractor exposures. Offer a free 'gap map' on two live projects using their subcontract warranty clause and OEM quotes. Target: three pilots at about $25K per project and one signed OEM rider negotiation. Confirm the key assumption early, which is what share of their data center equipment is contractor-furnished.

title: Neutral Baselines and Neighbor Guarantees for Data Centers
one_liner: A neutral third party installs pre-construction sensors around proposed data centers and administers a developer-funded, automatic payout guarantee to neighbors, so permit fights run on evidence.
customer: Independent and mid-size data center developers seeking 50-500 MW campus approvals in contested counties. County commissions and state regulators are a second buyer because they can make the service a permit condition. Hyperscalers with in-house community teams are not the target.
problem: Permit fights are evidence-poor. Nobody has a pre-construction baseline of well levels, night-time noise, air quality or voltage at homes, so every later complaint about dry wells or a hum can be neither proven nor disproven. Both sides fight on feelings and lawyers. Politics has turned: New York paused environmental permits for data centers of 50 MW or more in July 2026, Texas ordered its environmental regulator to stop issuing new data center permits in September 2026, and local pauses now exist in at least 14 states. A Reuters/Ipsos poll found only 14% of Americans would welcome one nearby.
solution: Baseline-in-a-Box. Over 60-90 days before the application, deploy 30-60 low-cost sensors: property-line night noise, depth and conductivity in volunteer neighbors' wells, PM2.5, night-sky brightness, and voltage sag at homes. Publish a read-only public dashboard. Have a university extension hydrogeologist and an acoustician review the methods. Escrow the data with hash-anchored timestamps so neither side can edit it. Keep monitoring for 10 years. Then add a Neighbor Guarantee: a developer-funded escrow that pays affected households automatically, like parametric crop insurance, when verified well drawdown or noise exceedances occur. No lawsuit is needed.
why_now: In 2026 the moratorium movement jumped from town boards to governors' offices (New York's executive order of July 14, Texas's TCEQ permit halt of September 21). Developers now need social license as much as megawatts, and regulators are actively drafting the frameworks that will say what evidence counts.
revenue_model: The developer pays $75-150k per site for setup, $4-10k per month for monitoring, and an 8-10% administration fee on the guarantee escrow. Counties that write the service into permit conditions create repeat demand. Later, anonymized data licensing to regulators and insurers.
non_obvious_insight: The baseline protects the developer more than the opponents. It is the only defense against future exaggerated or mistaken claims, and it turns 'trust us' into 'audit us'. Parametric payouts replace adversarial claims, which is why a rational developer buys it from a neutral party rather than opposing it.
first_30_days: Pick one county with a pending rezoning hearing (Georgia, Virginia, Indiana, Pennsylvania or Texas). Offer the developer's land agent a free 30-day pilot on 10 neighbor wells with an agricultural-extension partner. Build nodes from off-the-shelf parts at about $1.5-3k each. Present the live dashboard at the public hearing and convert that developer to a paid contract. Use the result as the case study for the next 5 developers.

title: Ride-Through Witness: Measure-First Large-Load Network
one_liner: Invert the parent's model-before-energization: ingest the UPS logs and power-quality waveforms sites already record, join them with grid-side PMU data, and auto-produce ISO-format ride-through and oscillation reports, growing into the reference data network that ISOs, OEMs and insurers rely on.
customer: Wedge: reliability and compliance managers and facility engineering leads at operators of 25-200 MW neocloud and colo sites in ERCOT and PJM, already energized or energizing. Second-side payers later are ISOs and TOs (aggregate feeds and model-validation reports), UPS and power-shelf OEMs (fleet analytics), and insurers.
problem: When a grid fault drops hundreds of MW of data center load, the ISO asks every site whether it tripped and why. The evidence sits inside the facility: UPS event logs, PQ-meter waveforms, power-shelf telemetry and transfer-to-backup thresholds. ISO PMUs only see the outside. As I read the reported 2024 Northern Virginia loss of about 1.5 GW, its cause was facility-side protection and backup-transfer behavior that grid operators could not see (verify against the NERC incident review). Pre-energization models are never validated against reality, and they decay as GPU firmware and UPS settings change monthly. Operators face blame, curtailment and NOGRR282 exposure with no forensic evidence and no ride-through margin figure.
solution: Software-first, with no hardware in the first release. 'Witness' ingests existing data (UPS event logs, PQDIF and COMTRADE files from existing PQ meters and relays, generator and BESS logs) and time-aligns it with public ISO and PMU frequency data. Within 24 hours of any event it generates an ISO-format disturbance report: what tripped, at what threshold and delay, how fast load recovered, and the oscillation signature. It also runs a continuous dashboard against NOGRR282 thresholds and detects GPU-cluster synchronized swings. Phase 2 adds a white-label certified point-on-wave recorder for sites without one. Phase 3 turns fleet data into measurement-validated models, a model-versus-reality score, OEM firmware benchmarks and an insurance risk score. We offer the report schema to ISOs and NERC as a standard, the equivalent of the IBR event-analysis and monitoring standards (PRC-028/029/030).
why_now: NOGRR282 has been in force since Aug 1, 2026, so the industry moves from modeling to operations, and the first real ride-through events at AI sites are being recorded now. NERC's IBR standards (PRC-028/029/030) show the regulatory template of monitoring plus event analysis for inverter-based resources, and it is plausible to extend it to large loads (unverified). GPU-load oscillation is now a public concern. Every operator already logs the data, and cheap cloud compute plus LLM-assisted log parsing make ingesting heterogeneous vendor formats cheap for the first time.
revenue_model: Operators: $30-70k per site per year for the subscription, or $10-15k per retro-analysis or event report. ISOs and TOs: $100-500k per year each for aggregated feeds and model-validation reports once 30 or more sites are connected. OEMs: $50-200k per year for cross-brand fleet analytics. Insurers: risk-score licensing. Data network effects and standard-setting are what make this a 10x outcome, with 300 sites at $50k as $15M in operator revenue alone, plus roughly the same again from the other sides.
non_obvious_insight: The 2024 event was an inside-the-facility information problem, and only the join of facility recorders and grid PMUs establishes causation. No single site sees aggregate risk, and only a neutral third party can pool data across UPS brands and operators, which OEMs and hyperscalers will not. That gives network economies and a cornered resource, proprietary as-measured behavior of real AI facilities in real faults. The parent sells the exam and this sells the proof you keep passing it. Free generic models cannot substitute for a fleet-wide, as-measured dataset. A retro-analysis of an operator's own past voltage dips is a sellable product with no OEM or pre-energization model required.
first_30_days: Sell a $10-15k Ride-Through Margin Audit built from an operator's own historical voltage-dip and UPS-transfer events, delivered by hand as a concierge service. Recruit one power-quality or protection engineer and one data engineer. Build parsers for PQDIF, COMTRADE and two or three UPS log formats. Contact reliability and compliance leads at 20 operators (ERCOT and PJM) and 3 TO or ISO planners, and offer a free report on one public event to each. Publish the draft report schema and an open primer on GPU oscillation signatures. Confirm what NOGRR282 requires in terms of operations-phase reporting.

competition_context:
Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: Typhoon HIL (Data Centers solution), OPAL-RT (HYPERSIM, power-HIL), EPRI DCFlex, Emerald AI (Emerald Conductor). White space: Across this session's research I found no direct competitor selling packaged, hardware-validated large-load dynamic models (PSS/E plus EMT) with ride-through study reports and certification letters for GPU-cluster, PSU and UPS stacks. Nobody was seen selling OEM-level type-test certification for power shelves and UPS platforms. Adjacent players cover only pieces: HIL tools (Typhoon HIL, OPAL-RT), generic EMT consultancies, EPRI's flexibility consortium, workload-flex software (Emerald AI), and simulation software vendors with no data center library shown.

Three structural threats need answers:
1. Regulators and EPRI or NERC may publish free generic composite or EMT models, which commoditizes the model library.
2. OEMs (UPS, PSU, NVIDIA) own the confidential control details and may ship their own models.
3. Per-project EMT consulting already exists and is not verified either way for large loads.

The defensible white space is independent, hardware-validated, ISO-acceptable model packages and compliance evidence for the 25-500 MW neocloud and colo developers who lack in-house power simulators. It would be reused across sites through OEM platform type tests, not sold as bespoke studies.

Research limits: the WebSearch budget (200 calls) was exhausted before this task began, so competitor discovery relied on direct page fetches and GitHub search. Startup databases (Crunchbase, YC, Product Hunt), news, and NERC or EPRI publication pages were not checked. Several NERC, EPRI and PJM URLs returned 404 or empty content. Treat the 'no direct competitor' finding as moderate-confidence. Verify manually against NERC LLTF outputs, EPRI data center model reports, and WECC or ERCOT model requirements before committing. | How this version avoids them: Typhoon HIL and OPAL-RT are pre-deployment lab and simulation tools. This is post-energization and field-measured. Emerald AI throttles and shifts load, and we measure and prove behavior. EPRI DCFlex runs nine demonstration sites and is a consortium, not a commercial fleet dataset, and it is a likely standards partner. Electranix, Danovo and Pearl Street sell project-based studies before energization. Hyperscaler in-house work is out of scope because our first customers are those without it. The unresearched risk is power-quality monitoring vendors, which sell hardware and generic dashboards. We ingest their files and become the analytics and ISO-reporting layer on top, and they may also be a hardware channel.
